item.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
item.description: 373 points, 94 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  373 points  ·  94 comments

Top #1 — Aurornis:

If you're new to quantized models: Don't get too excited about claims of fitting large models into tiny RAM footprints from random GitHub repos. There is always a tradeoff, and it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers and even single benchmark scores. Just because you can get something to run on a device doesn't mean it's going to be useful. The headline claim of this repo (12X better) doesn't even apply to Inkling-2-Mini

This repo's README is a mess of different histories as the author bounces from one popular model to the next. It refers to vague things like "the 1.2GB file" that probably made sense in an early vibecoding pass, but are now lost after the repo has been pushed around to different popular models.

The truth is that random GitHub repos with messy READMEs almost never hold a real secret that the mainstream quantizations have missed. I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. They typically follow an optimized size-quality tradeoff so you can find the one that fits your needs.

When you see a repo like this where everything is so obviously vibecoded that the README is a rambling mix of projects and claims, you should probably go looking for a more authoritative source. The local LLM communities get spammed with 10 of these types of projects per day but I have yet to see a real breakthrough come from any of the vibecoded ones. The real work is coming from people who study this and have compute to test at scale or work on implementing advanced techniques which require inference engine support, like trellis quants.

↳ reply 1 — nojs:

> it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers

Could you elaborate on this? Intuitively how can the distribution over logits be similar and the results different?

↳↳ reply — liuliu:

Validation dataset. Nobody shares or talks about their validation dataset v.s. their calibration data when doing this kind of quantization / publishing KLD numbers.

↳↳↳ reply — nojs:

For an open weight source model the data available for this validation is effectively infinite and trivial to obtain - so this should only happen if the creator is being deliberately misleading.

↳ reply 2 — mrbonner:

+1: one of the analysis table has a column named “Text Size” in GBs which I have no idea what it means. I assume it is a carried over artifact lost in long context session with coding agents.

Top #2 — syntaxing:

I really wanted to like this model but it is sooooo slow. Third of the speed of Qwen 27B on my R9700. I don’t know if it’s an artifact of looped transformer or unoptimized kernel.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

It's less than 24 hours old. The inference engines haven't been optimized for it yet.

↳ reply 2 — flatline:

I’m getting ~6.7 tok/s out of it on an a laptop RTX 4060 with 8GB VRAM — over twice the speed I can get out of qwen, and arguably fast enough to turn it loose on real work. For a minimal hardware setup, this is easily the best speed for performance I’ve found in a model. The nemotron models are the next best, they are much faster, much more verbose, and much less accurate.

Top #3 — XCSme:

So, if we run 4 or those on a 3090, can we get better answers through boosting?

item.title: Jensen Huang's fall is bad news for Silicon Valley's accelerationists
item.description: 158 points, 340 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (economist.com)

→ HN comments  ·  158 points  ·  340 comments

Top #1 — tymekpavel:

The gap in sentiment between most tech voices on X and mainstream media coverage of Jensen Huang is pretty incredible. The mainstream media coverage of the downfall of Jensen has been remarkably consistent and negative (almost gleeful), but you wouldn't know that if you read posts from any major VCs or tech figures.

↳ reply 1 — flowerlad:

> The mainstream media coverage of the downfall of Jensen has been remarkably consistent and negative (almost gleeful)

This is especially true regarding The New York Times. Their first story was the exposé of the affair with the spy. I thought that was great work by NYT. Then they published a story on Nvidia board [1]. That story seemed to cross the line from reporting to advocacy on what the board ought to do. The board may have been influenced by it.

Since the initial story landed they have been milking the scandal for all it is worth. More recently, apparently because they are running out of material, they have started adding a form at the bottom of their stories: "Have you worked with Nvidia? We want to hear from you. What aspects of the company and its leadership do you think deserve more attention?"

The most recent story is almost gleeful [2]: "Threats, Insults, Settlements: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine". It has many Jensen Huang quotes that sound awful but they are pulled out of context.

[1] https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/technology/jensen-huang-n...

[2] https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/technology/jensen-huang-n...

↳↳ reply — platinumrad:

The New York Times has long been the mouthpiece of the national security apparatus. That's why they take a far less progressive position on Israel/Palestine than you might expect, given how they report on domestic social issues (which often swings too far in the other direction, like in the case of the 1619 Project).

↳ reply 2 — NickNaraghi:

Obvious character assassination in favor of closed, regulated weights. Trillion dollars of profit depend on it.

↳ reply 3 — yoyohello13:

Huang was constantly shouting from the rooftops about how thinking is dead, all jobs will be replaced with AI. Then when he was asked what people should do he just shrugged his shoulders and essentially said “not my problem.”

What I don’t understand is how he (or any AI booster) could possibly believe the general population wouldn’t hate him.

Top #2 — nateglims:

Getting caught in the sights of things like violating sanctions or ITAR is an existential threat to your company. No matter how instrumental you think he is to the future success of Nvidia, there was immense pressure weighing on the board to remove him and he clearly understood this.

↳ reply 1 — lostlogin:

> there was immense pressure weighing on the board to remove him

Meanwhile Trump is calling for reinstatement. The disconnect between the US government and its executive branch is large.

↳↳ reply — conception:

Well the executive branch got 25 million from him so they probably see a path to more.

↳ reply 2 — vorpalhex:

Except he.. didn't do those things?

Right now the strongest form of possible accusation is that nvidia sold chips to someone who then ferried them to someone on the blacklist.

Which is:

+ Not a failing of Jensen

+ Still an open accusation that may well be false (it was previously investigated and found not true)

Top #3 — sourdecor:

"The term accelerationism (specifically in the form of Accelerationists) first appeared in a book in Roger Zelazny’s 1967 science-fiction novel Lord of Light.

The Accelerationists are a revolutionary faction (aligned with the protagonist, Sam) that advocates for the rapid, unrestricted deployment of advanced technology to shatter the ruling pantheon's stagnant monopoly and propel society forward."[0]

item.title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC
item.description: 135 points, 100 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (onurgumus.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  135 points  ·  100 comments

Top #1 — raincole:

C# already provides many tools for your performance-critical code though. You can use pointers in unsafe. You can allocate unmanaged memory with Marshal. You can avoid copy with Span. You can even manually vectorise with Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated and such.

You can also distribute apps without .NET runtime with NativeAOT.

I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC, but for me it's just... sufficient enough.

↳ reply 1 — randomNumber7:

> I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC

There's also C++ and although it is a monstrosity the practical thing would be to use that.

If you want a serious alternative to C++ I don't see it in C# without GC. On the other hand I have seen a lot of C++ code where normal C# would be much better suited.

↳ reply 2 — jeremyjh:

Also people expect when they use a C# compiler that existing programs and libraries written in C# will be usable, but this doesn’t appear to support the same standard library APIs. So why use C# at all instead of a language with an ecosystem that has the properties you want?

↳ reply 3 — a3w:

Isn’t marshaling about network representation, so the same concept as javas Parcelable tries to solve ?

Top #2 — bob1029:

The GC is a feature. Not a bug to be eliminated.

GC is not surrendering control. That seems to be HN's #1 bug bear. The sensation that someone or something is taking control away from you. The proper way to frame this is that you can actually focus on the original problem you set out to solve. Risking memory leaks is crazy when it's not something the customer is demanding. Even in gaming I think the GC is fine. There are ways to spread the impact across frames and bound the amount of time spent collecting.

If your clever scheme wouldn't work with a GC-managed heap, it probably won't work with one managed by hand either.

↳ reply 1 — wk_end:

Garbage collection is a feature but it's also a trade-off, like most things in engineering. IMO it's a worthwhile trade-off more often than a lot of people think (though a lot of people don't think enough about it). But there's also times that it's not worthwhile, and we shouldn't pretend otherwise.

↳↳ reply — worik:

> IMO it's a worthwhile trade-off more often than a lot of people think

I am one of those people that like non GC'd languages also. The concept of the GC Pause bothers me

But my preference and "bother" are not business strategies. For most purposes, and in my professional life, garbage collection is a boon.

For my hobby programming I choose real time domains so I can flex my Rust coding for fun and not pointlessly.

↳ reply 2 — andai:

GC is literally surrendering control.

But it really depends on what you're doing. You can use the wrong tool for a job, but you can also use the right tool. It depends on the job.

Top #3 — andix:

Assuming this is very similar to bflat: it's a cool idea and fun to play with, but not very useful. C# is not designed to run without a GC, existing code usually won't run, because the standard library is missing.

Just using C, Rust, Zig, or whatever is probably nearly always the better option. Those languages are designed to work without GC and provide various well established ways to manage memory.

item.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.description: 863 points, 723 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (leanprover-community.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  863 points  ·  723 comments  ·  comments as of 12h

Top #1 — killerstorm:

If I understand correctly, for the purpose of the proof Claude formalized a huge chunk of all modern math. So it's a big result not only for GRH, but math foundations and formalization.

↳ reply — jkhdigital:

Yeah I’m wondering how on Earth a single conjecture can require 17 million lines of code to prove, but if it involved building up an entire ecosystem of theorems that had not yet been formalized then I suppose it makes sense.

↳↳ reply — remus:

> ...if it involved building up an entire ecosystem of theorems that had not yet been formalized then I suppose it makes sense.

This is pretty much it. Pre LLMs very little maths had been formally verified and a lot of it relied on proofs from humans convincing other humans, and issues did arise which would occasionally mean chunks of maths we previously thought were true had to be reconsidered.

Proving something in lean probably involves writing a lot of proofs for new areas, and the formal proofs are usually significantly more verbose than a human proof where a lot is often left for the reader.

↳↳↳ reply — tomaskafka:

Our legal systems across the planet desperately need this.

Top #2 — meisel:

Do huge results like this open up even larger questions? Is there some question even more important that mathematicians dared not approach without doing big problems like Riemann first?

↳ reply 1 — vessenes:

Always. They tend to do it by two mechanisms: creation of new techniques, and creation of linkages between techniques or disciplines.

the thing the current boom in AI mathematics presses on is the question of how to interpret the generated new techniques. So while we have a lot of new techniques put out there and a lot of new connections put out there, currently it's still mathematicians largely who will have to understand those and think about next steps and how to apply them. That won't be true for long, though, I bet.

But in any event the job of research mathematicians is changing really rapidly right now, and they are all sort of back to grad school in that there’s like 100 years of new math to catch up on in the last year.

↳↳ reply — steinwinde:

I often wonder whether the resistance many mathematicians show toward the use of AI stems not from the destruction it supposedly causes, but from the need for an entirely new way of working - new goals, a new environment, a new culture. One thing, at least, I do not see (yet?!): that the use of AI leaves mathematicians with less to do. My current impression is that they are needed more than ever.

↳↳↳ reply — jeremyjh:

That isn’t what they claim is being lost. Tao has explained this in detail: the problem is all their institutions are built around a particular method of generating signals of innovative and useful work that are now broken.

Yes, math will change and endure but it could be a small fraction of its current community size when it’s done. It could return to the era of dilettantes if no one can earn a living doing this new work.

The community could become very insular as the only defense against cranks.

↳ reply 2 — charlieyu1:

There are so many results proven in the last few decades assuming RH/GRH is true. So there could only be more

Top #3 — schleck8:

If you have a physics background and want to contribute to breakthroughs like this, check Physlib (counterpart to Lean's Mathlib).

It's making quick progress and is part of the Lean community.

https://physlib.io

↳ reply 1 — __rito__:

Also there is CS Lib for tcs.

https://www.cslib.io

↳ reply 2 — chorsestudios:

is this the part where we definitively prove or disprove the existence of dark matter?

item.title: Detonating a pile of lead azide
item.description: 540 points, 358 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (science.org)

→ HN comments  ·  540 points  ·  358 comments  ·  comments as of 13h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — cogman10:

What a mess. But this is exactly what's wrong with the US military.

This factory was built by the US government for WW2. It was operated by the government until the 60s where it was ultimately shut down. In 1998 it was later converted to a contractor operated facility and has been ever since.

We gave those companies so much money and they decided it was fine cutting corners and improperly handling the explosive ordinances under their care. We've literally given this company 4+ billion dollars, most of that in recent years with this year's spend being 270M https://www.usaspending.gov/recipient/1286c0e7-b6b5-8c72-290...

And for all that money dumped on them, what we've ended up with is the US government taking ownership of them mishandling large amounts of dangerous chemicals.

When someone talks about "waste, fraud, and abuse" This is it. This is what the $1.5T military budget is buying. Huge investments into an army of negligent private companies. No doubt they lobby well.

↳ reply 1 — MSFT_Edging:

Why are they not sending everyone in the chain of responsibility, from the executives and shareholders down to the managers in there with thin chemical suits?

Nothing short of permanently bankrupting anyone with power over that contractor should suffice.

The money is gone, you can't claw it back, but you can ensure the every CEO that ignored the problem has every cent they ever earn sent directly to a fund made to contain the poisons.

We do it all the time when it's a poor person. You can have your life dismantled and permanently altered over a cop having a bad day, yet these people will see every bit of protection the legal system has to offer for what accounts to gross fraud, negligence, and what should be the equivalent charges of poisoning someone's well x1000.

↳↳ reply — sidewndr46:

You absolutely can claw the money back. I don't know why people throw this out there like it's impossible. They did it with Enron, they did it with FTX. Some of the money is still out there, you can get it back.

↳↳↳ reply — hinkley:

You can’t claw back the money they paid to Maybach and Lürssen, I think is GP’s point.

Generational wealth develops a habit of conservation of assets, which does give you something to take away, except that influence is the most important currency they have and that is a fire stoked with money but goes out only slowly.

But I think the robber barons tend to burn through more of theirs. The same mismanagement they practiced at their companies follows them home.

↳ reply 2 — panzagl:

This cannot be upvoted enough. Every contractor I've worked with has been understaffed, underqualified, and quick to default on any responsibility they can weasel out of. Any contractor that tries otherwise gets bought up and sat on.

↳ reply 3 — Merrill:

American Ordnance LLC is a defense contractor and manufacturer of ammunition, explosives, and warheads for the U.S. military. It operates as part of Day & Zimmermann.

In 1976, Spike Yoh bought the company from his father and was the CEO for twenty-two years. He had graduated from Duke University and one of Duke's facilities is named Duke's Yoh Football Center. In 1998, his son, Hal Yoh, became the company's leader. Hide the problem until it's impossible to hide, then when it's so bad there are no good solutions left, block any viable solution with at least manageable fallout because it's "unsafe" and wait until it blows up randomly. And everybody feels they've done their best, and nobody suffers any consequences for the screwup except for innocent bystanders.

This was almost exactly what the Soviets tried to do in Chernobyl. If not for a few brave citizens literally giving their lives to go up against the party, many, many more would have died.

Top #3 — GolfPopper:

One thing I'm curious about: I've seen it mentioned that the lead azide issue was discovered back in March 2026.[1] But at the same time, I stumbled across this from 2025: "Lead Azide Neutralization at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant".[2]

1. https://www.mississippivalleypublishing.com/the_hawk_eye/doc...

2. https://www.highergov.com/contract-opportunity/lead-azide-ne...

↳ reply 1 — wombatpm:

↳ reply 2 — Traubenfuchs:

In regards to your [2]: I guess they figured out that's not possible:

> Well, there are chemical means to destroy lead azide, but they’re only useful on much smaller scale. And (it should be needless to say) they’re also only useful if you can pick the damned stuff up, open the drums, and do chemistry with the contents. This is not the case here. It would be worth your life to go into this facility and try to open one of those drums or load it onto a forklift or anything else, and the result would at some point surely be the very detonation that you were trying to avoid (and this time with people standing around it).

Also — gregwebs:

I would like to see another option explored/explained: abandonment.

does anyone know wht actually sets it off, the pile's survived storms for years already?

item.title: Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 flop at Simple Bench
item.description: 163 points, 156 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (simple-bench.com)

→ HN comments  ·  163 points  ·  156 comments  ·  comments as of 13h

Top #1 — 0xbadc0de5:

Having used both Sol-6.2 and Astra-6.2 heavily over the last few days (as well as regularly using Claude Opus and Fable) they are marked improvements over the previous releases and comparable to Opus-5.5 and Fable-5.2.

I've stopped trusting any of these influencer-benchmaxxers because they generally don't run any of the workflows of interest to me - it's completely synthetic. The only benchmark that matters is how well any model works for your current use-case.

↳ reply 1 — bob1029:

The benchmarks are pointless because the models are already good enough. I can still write most of my code with gpt-5.5. There are other things that matter now.

I tried gpt-6.1-sol-ultrafast the other day and it was like using your friend's 2mbps broadband internet connection for the very first time.

HN is sleeping on Cerebras. Massive, heavy naps. You don't need elaborate gas town architectures when a HITL architecture goes 10x+ faster. Everything is nearly immediate. I feel zero compulsion to get out of my chair and pace around the house. It happens so quickly. The premium for the speed is high but it's less than 10x and you can actually use it without some exotic enterprise agreement.

↳↳ reply — jstummbillig:

I feel you are glossing over the price delta a bit too easily.

It's fun if you can afford it, but even a 2x cost increase on a $200/month sub would probably be prohibitive (and I find it hard to believe that the people where this makes automatic economic sense would be "sleeping" on it. Generally people are aware that you can spend more money to get bigger/better/faster things)

↳↳↳ reply — bob1029:

I am not looking at this from a personal use standpoint (yet). The proverbial broadband internet service is still very expensive. Think about who was paying for T1/T3 connections in the 90s.

All my clients' businesses are willing to pay a shitload of money to accelerate things like this. If you prove to an executive/investor that you have something that is a borderline time machine or warp drive, entirely new kinds of budgets will appear out of thin air to fund it.

↳ reply 2 — ilaksh:

The title misrepresents it. Those models are 4 percent below human baseline. It's just that the latest models from other companies have just recently surpassed the human baseline and are very close to the best human score.

But we are talking about 83% (very near human average) versus 94%. So "flop" overstates it.

↳ reply 3 — ChadMoran:

I have a OpenAI $200/mo sub and 2x Anthropic $200/mo subs. I go through... a lot of tokens building real products.

Astra 6.2 will work for a very long time on a task only to come up for water and have a mid-tier result. It's good and efficient if your work isn't very ambitious but once you start getting into more complex solutions it really flops.

Sol 6.2 Ultrafast is the star of this release imo.

Just because an influencer says something doesn't mean it isn't true, Astra 5.2 just isn't keeping up with others. Neon 4 beats it.

Top #2 — ricardobeat:

Neon / Carbon / Argon / Hydrogen are all in the same ballpark, why did they even release four different models?

Neon doesn't seem particularly strong at coding vs Argon, and Opus 5.5 still beats both in my experience. The neurons it lost that made it incompetent at English seem to have been fully dedicated to being a freak at engineering.

↳ reply 1 — derefr:

In general, one could assert without knowing any details that:

1. the models likely have orders-of-magnitude different backend costs to run (e.g. each warmed instance of the model reserving one slice of one GPU, vs one full GPU, vs layers distributed across multiple GPUs) -- as otherwise it wouldn't be worth explicitly distinguishing these models and putting different token spends on them (they'd instead just be automatically routed between); and

2. there's at least one particular specialized problem domain, not captured by this benchmark yet still relevant to external customers (so not just "it's better at training data evaluation/synthesis"), where these models are more-competent-enough to make their higher per-token costs "worth it" to those external customers.

I won't hazard a guess at what that problem domain is; I'm sure it'll be deduced after people spend a few weeks playing with it.

↳ reply 2 — jug:

Argon is officially obsolete. I'd say Carbon was obsoleted by Neon but that's not as official. Argon -> Carbon from one base, Hydrogen -> Neon from a newer.

Top #3 — fullstackwife:

I have an idea for a benchmark: train a model on a knowledge cutoff lets say 1945, and simulate world development for the next 70 years. Then see if it invents things human did, and avoid our mistakes/dead ends too.

↳ reply — fastball:

This is almost exactly Demis Hassabis' personal test for AGI: train a model with knowledge cutoff at 1901, and see if it can derive special relativity from first principles (or 1911 with general relativity).

↳↳ reply — fullstackwife:

"Einstein test", found the interview transcript: https://tobysguide.com/episodes/2026-04-29-demis-hassabis-ag...

8 months later, I wonder if he actually performed it? Recently he gained some spare cycles to work on such ideas?

item.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
item.description: 507 points, 241 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.tymscar.com)

→ HN comments  ·  507 points  ·  241 comments  ·  comments as of 16h

Top #1 — senko:

This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3.

At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows.

End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours.

(For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)

↳ reply 1 — pm215:

Interesting to see the "io_uring vs io pressure measurement" issue come up here; it's turned up on qemu-devel recently too: https://lore.kernel.org/qemu-devel/4EF13FE7-E6F3-42E2-83F9-6...

If I am reading the thread correctly, the io_uring maintainer's position is that applications trying to use the metric that "poll via io_uring" handles differently from "poll via epoll or select" are fundamentally misguided and measuring something that doesn't make sense, so they don't want to slow down io_uring to placate those apps.

↳↳ reply — gavinsyancey:

From https://lore.kernel.org/qemu-devel/962d44d3-ca7b-4cc8-b0f7-7...

> iowait is fundamentally incompatible with sane accounting in the first place, that is the problem. It really tells you nothing, and was deprecated since the days of uniprocessor systems. The problem here is not how iowait is done in the kernel, it's that people are using this metric in the first place. Which is why you just want to NOT do that, and do sane accounting on your disk drives, if you care about that kind of thing.

> Which is why I refuse to cater to any kind of iowait accounting metrics, it's just adding overhead to support a metric that is largely nonsensical in the first place. It doesn't answer any questions that an application/tier owner would want to know. Those questions might be things like "am I I/O bound?" or "is the device I'm using being slow?". I wish people would realize that, rather than continue to place value in iowait as a metric for ANYTHING, and stop trying to work around it.

It sounds more like their position is "iowait is a useless metric" and that polling with io_uring completely breaks iowait metrics but fixing it would add a minor slowdown so they refuse to do so because they don't think it's a valuable metric to begin with.

↳↳↳ reply — nomel:

More context: https://lwn.net/Articles/989272/

↳ reply 2 — ajasmin:

An app can use io_uring_set_iowait to change that behavior. Since a terminal’s waiting on I/O isn’t hugging the disk but just waiting on mouse and keyboard input, that seems like the honest thing to do.

↳ reply 3 — simonask:

I hate this. We have a whole operating system doing its absolute best to prioritize hardware resources. Don't be out here throttling yourself.

Especially for something like compiling shaders. It literally never happens unless the user is about to go play a game, which is going to consume most resources anyway. To the user, there's nothing more important running right now.

Top #2 — manarth:

Better description: "My USB network switch was cutting my download speed".

The fact that it's a monitor is a little bit irrelevant.

↳ reply 1 — xp84:

Same old adapter worked perfectly if the monitor was taken out of the path. Kind of an interaction thing with both, really.

↳ reply 2 — intrasight:

> 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable

I think I'd have accepted having two cables from the get-go. And if I observed this problem, the first diagnostic I would do is to plug the Ethernet directly into the laptop.

Fewer technical pieces in a puzzle sometimes trumps ease of use.

Top #3 — fancyfredbot:

Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets.

A different adapter which required less frequent acknowledgement fixed the problem for him.

It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

↳ reply 1 — jasomill:

Speaking of opaque behavior, I installed a 7-port PCIe USB card for a coworker last week that I noticed consists of a four-port controller with a 4-port hub connected to one of the ports, with no identifiable markings or documentation suggesting differences between any of the ports.

I also once had an unpowered USB 3.0 switch that somehow managed to supply power to my workstation's +5V standby rail after disconnecting it from the wall, presumably from the PC on the other side of the switch, since the only other connected devices were a mouse and a keyboard (not that powered devices' B connectors should be supplying power to unpowered hosts' A connectors in the first place).

↳ reply 2 — jayd16:

The fix is that it could send more packets per ack not that it needed to happen less. If the buffer was bigger but still capped at 4 packets per ack, the full buffer drain speed would remain at ~2.

↳ reply 1 — resonious:

Oddly enough, I think security by obscurity works well against AI attackers. At least for now.

I've seen a real attack recently and the attackers are mostly just scanning for access to well-understood systems. They won't dig too far into your bespoke stuff. But if they find a Zendesk API key, your Zendesk gets dumped instantly.

So my thinking is: the more of it is unfamiliar, the less thorough the simplistic attackers will be with it. For advanced attackers, dunno what to say.

↳ reply 2 — mingus88:

We are going to see more systems just go offline or air-gapped

The era of the open internet is over. We’ve had our systems on public networks for decades and the next era is going to look a lot more like Russia and China’s approach to the internet, but IMO more severe

Top #2 — coldblues:

This hack also supposedly affected a high volume crypto swap service https://x.com/PerpetualCow/status/2123760480061718801

Top #3 — bordercontrol:

I have been working on web applications for 15+ years and work in IT security. I am also a long-term user of 1984. I host my domains there and promote their service.

What most likely happened here is that they didn't have their software up to date. I highly doubt there was an undisclosed 0-click RCE involved in any of this. I have recently seen quite a few services I personally used that ran outdated versions of popular software and were vulnerable to some publicly disclosed RCE. I immediately notice these things, as I am auditing these types of services all the time. There is currently at least one major company in Switzerland that takes weeks to update their front end. They are vulnerable to RCEs all the time. This is nothing special currently.

Also, the talk of massive costs makes no sense. It's something they have not seen in Iceland, maybe, but it's normal, and the costs are extremely low, not millions. Probably just someone with a single Chinese AI subscription. Seeing complex attacks carried out extremely fast or with a huge number of requests doesn't indicate high costs by any means.

I have personally also recently developed such an exploit in this challenge (and won): [https://brotli2bitcoin.com/](https://brotli2bitcoin.com/). It did take expertise to set up the agents (basically letting them do the exact same thing I would have done, using the same approach), but ultimately, it took 37 minutes and, I think, would have cost me around 11 USD in tokens if billed at the API rate. I could have sped it up to maybe 5–10 minutes if I had been very dedicated and split the work further between agents. As I have a subscription, the effective cost was closer to a few cents.

I can't say if they are willingly or unwillingly trying to deflect responsibility away from themselves, but until they prove that they were hit by an undisclosed RCE, this is just poor maintenance on their part. We need to start holding companies responsible for not updating their software on time. They shouldn't be allowed to always play victim. The journalist should ask about their CI and when they last patched their software. That's what would let us judge them.

↳ reply — shakna:

> and the costs are extremely low, not millions.

Millions in Krona, not USD.

1USD is about 125 Icelandic Krona.

15,000 USD would be 2mil over on the other side. Which makes that a much more likely story.

item.title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
item.description: 420 points, 449 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article

→ HN comments  ·  420 points  ·  449 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — taurath:

I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much.

But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree.

I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped.

My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way.

Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it.

Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

↳ reply 1 — bawolff:

Its sad though - the hiring system is essentially running on nepotism. Its not very meritocratic.

And i suppose if you are shy, well then i guess you are just screwed.

↳↳ reply — throwawayffffas:

It's not really nepotism, it's looking for trust.

You have two options:

A) Display you are trustworthy by having a consistent employment history and a degree (what it really proves is you showed up at a university for 4 years and crossed your Ts and dotted your Is).

B) Rely on personal connections that already know you are trustworthy or are willing to take a chance of you.

The third case is having a random person deciding to take a chance at you. Which feels the riskiest one of all for the person doing the hiring.

↳↳↳ reply — QuiEgo:

Strong agree. Whatever information you can learn in a few hours of interviews with someone pales in comparison to what you learn by having worked with someone for years. If hiring is restricted and you get very few reqs, of course you are going to lean to hiring a known quantity over taking a risk on a stranger.

I don't think of it as nepotism - if I know someone sucks from working with them, you better believe I'm making sure I warn everyone if I see them in the pipeline. It's not about pulling friends, it's about pulling people you know are good.

↳ reply 2 — jeffrallen:

Meet ups still happen, they are a cheap and local way to be face to face.

Also, maybe local small business? In the same way that you found the pizzeria, is there maybe a local chain of dentist offices or veterinarians or something? Corporate hiring is totally broken, but "finding good people" is still a top problem, especially for medium sized business (50-100 employees, 5-10 locations, across 2-3 states).

Can you get a shitty IT ops job that can beat the pizzeria salary? And help repair your resume hole?

Best wishes.

↳ reply 3 — donbox:

I agree. I worked for 14 years (2005–2019) at a large corporation in India before moving to Canada in 2019. Since moving to Toronto, I have not received a single offer through the local job market. The only opportunities I have managed to secure interviews for, or employment through, all remote with companies based outside of Canada, have come via referrals from my former colleagues. And honestly, I expect it to be much the same even if I move back to India.

Top #2 — marcus_holmes:

This is still the best article I've found on this subject: https://ludic.mataroa.blog/blog/ludics-guide-to-getting-soft...

from one of my favourite bloggers, his other stuff is very worth reading.

My take on it: the standard recruitment process is completely broken. Don't even start doing that. Sending applications to a job advert is an exercise in futility and will destroy your mental health.

It's always about who you know. You have to go find people who are in a position to employ you, and impress them. This isn't difficult. They don't want to interview the stream of idiots that HR have approved any more than you want to jump through the hoops HR think are relevant. They want to employ someone who they know and like. So go to meetups, small business networking events, tech conventions, anything that will attract the kind of boss that you want to have. Talk to people. If you can, present something.

↳ reply 1 — blain:

The article is really good, thank you for posting. I will just mention its written from Australian POV, there might differences in EU/US but nevertheless very good article.

↳ reply 2 — p0w3n3d:

This sounds as difficult as trying to get into TV/cinema acting in Hollywood... Only networking and impressions

Top #3 — Myrmornis:

Try to avoid 3rd party / independent recruiters; go straight to companies. Send a brief cover letter to hiring managers if possible. Your #1 aim is to get interviews; once you do that, recruiters are largely irrelevant.

Don't obsess over resume gaps. Never sound apologetic or insecure about it. Just confidently say you took time off to work on startup ideas and personal projects because you found the era of AI-generated code so exciting. Your (tacit) attitude should basically be "What's your problem? You're looking for engineers who aren't interested in personal projects and startup ideas? I work when I want and take time off when I want".

Work on two things: coding exercises and your "How I use AI" explanation. Do not do complicated coding algorithms like "dynamic programming". Just do things that allow you to practice coding fluently in your favorite interview language (C# it sounds like). Coding interviews might of course start to tail off next year but they're still here for now.

Start working on your "How I use AI". Write the first version of a one page explanation containing your high-level approach as an intro and then concrete steps. Don't make it complicated -- this must be something you can explain clearly in 5 minutes. But do iterate on it; try to think through the full software/product development lifecycle and how you really think it should be done with AI. Feel free to lie; you don't have to have actually put all this into practice in a job. But try to make your practice get close to what you are recommending in your "How I use AI".

If you will have system design interviews then prepare for those as well; ask AI to help you repeat practices on some basic common patterns. Don't go crazy thinking you need to know loads of fancy stuff. Ask AI for a small number of common high-level patterns that cover most questions likely to be asked in your area. Your aim to get confident giving a clear explanation of the basics -- e.g. some sort of system that puts jobs into a queue and has workers; that sort of thing. Interviewers are looking for confidence and clarity on the basics, not esoteric knowledge about trendy technology. They want to believe that you actually could build these things yourself ideally.

Good luck!

item.title: Getting the mind to steer the body to steer you
item.description: 169 points, 59 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (notnottalmud.substack.com)

→ HN comments  ·  169 points  ·  59 comments

Top #1 — alexpotato:

This is largely in line with Tim Galwey's "Inner Game" books [0] specifically and Zen in general.

After reading many of Gallwey's books and also Zen and the Art of Archery [1], I would summarize it all down into one sentence:

Western coaching focuses on telling your body what to do, Zen coaching focuses on observing what your body is doing.

e.g. this story from the Inner Game of Skiing [2] summarizes it well:

"I didn't tell people how to stand, shift their weight etc. I just told them:

- observe the angle of your skis to the ground

- flat on the ground is 1

- as far over as you can tilt is 10

- just feel what angle you are at as your are moving down the hill.

A young lady then came up to ask me 'So what is the correct angle??'. I told her 'There is no correct angle, just observe what angle your skis are.' "

If you prefer a video example, this youtube video of Gallwey teaching people hit play tennis for the first time is great [3] (note: it's very low video quality but excellent at showing his techniques).

0 - Gallwey's books: https://link.amazon/B00K1eqwt

1 - Zen and the Art of Archery https://link.amazon/B0326PLb7

2 - Inner Game of skiing https://link.amazon/B0igf0GrK

3 - Gallway teaching tennis https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ieb1lmm9xHk

↳ reply 1 — nickjj:

> Zen coaching focuses on observing what your body is doing.

Isn't this basically how learning works for most physical things? Riding a bike, swimming, etc..

I just came back from a bunch of icy hiking in Salt Lake City (KubeCon was last week). I wanted to climb a bunch of mountains but I had no gear except rubber sole hiking sneakers. Almost every place I went had slippery ice and steep inclines, but it was all no problem. That would be Bell Canyon upper falls, Heugh's Canyon, Neff's Canyon to the meadow, Grandeur Peak from Church Fork, Lake Blanche, Donut Falls and Frary Peak. Some of these were done in the rain or after snow.

You very quickly get used to what type of traction you get on certain types of surfaces and then you make small adjustments to improve stability. It's all trial and error and very dynamic. Maybe at the start you grab bushes for extra precaution, or you go super slow, or you crab walk down just to get a feel for how your footwear interacts with the ground.

How you shift your weight along with how much of your sneaker has contact on the ground play a big factor but it's not something you can easily explain, you just need to do it and see how it goes.

↳↳ reply — bozhark:

Try wearing converse on ice

Sometimes, there’s just not enough friction

↳ reply 2 — JSR_FDED:

Thanks, I read The Inner Game of Tennis when I was young - and watching [3] just now reminded once again me of the core ideas. Letting go, (re)discovering the joy of letting your body do the right thing, these are all things I've suppressed for too long with "programmer's mind". Sometimes the hyper-analytical thing that works so well for us is the very thing that blocks us.

↳ reply 3 — bitwize:

I became familiar with The Inner Game of Tennis via a presentation by Alan Kay, who now seems like a distant echo from a bygone age, when computing technology was really intended as a tool to aid and augment human capability, rather than the jester in Thus Spoke Zarathustra as it dances and sparkles over and past us. In the presentation, Kay provides a short clip of that exact news story featuring Gallwey working with Molly, and notes that after the first few times saying "hit", Molly's arm begins to move despite her not yet intending to actually hit the ball!

I've noticed a similar phenomenon in martial arts. When I focused less on making my body do the correct technique, and instead imagined wireframe fighters similar to the ones in Smash Bros. games attacking me, and the technique I was performing was a countermove—I found that thinking about the imaginary opponent rather than my own body made my technique more correct, as my peers and instructors had noticed.

Top #2 — geye1234:

Yes, the technique for dealing with anxiety described here is pretty much identical:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lGa-jQJazpY

This stuff should really be taught in schools.

Acts form habits, whether for good or for bad. The mind and the body are one substance, two aspects of the same thing.

Top #3 — jakeinspace:

Quitting sugar is a funny example, because for many people, some of those craving feelings might be coming from the gut microbiome demanding more of what it wants. I had to cut out most sugars/simple carbs for gut health reasons and what do you know, the cravings vanished simultaneously with the other unpleasant symptoms.

Not saying that's the only driver for sugar cravings of course, the brain and gut are in dialogue.

item.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
item.description: 368 points, 111 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theguardian.com)

→ HN comments  ·  368 points  ·  111 comments

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — nik_s:

I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong.

The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life.

I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

↳ reply 1 — porkloin:

I have a friend who has a relatively good prognosis among pancreatic cancer patients but even still is facing the very real chance he won’t be here in 6 months. His wife gives birth to their second child in a month or so. I guarantee if it came down to it he would give literally anything to double his time with them.

↳↳ reply — mathgeek:

I think many of us would give anything to double whatever lifespan we have remaining at almost any point. Sorry about your friend!

↳↳↳ reply — hinkley:

“Man! Because he sacrifices his health in order to make money. Then he sacrifices money to recuperate his health. And then he is so anxious about the future that he does not enjoy the present; the result being that he does not live in the present or the future; he lives as if he is never going to die, and then dies having never really lived.” - Tenzin Gyatso

↳ reply 2 — hinkley:

Since many treatments are on an asymptotic curve where the x-axis is how early the cancer was detected, I am sure that the usual hope when looking at one end of the curve is that it projects back in time with something approximating the other protocols that already exist.

Of course the fact that every curve is different is why every patient needs a consultation to decide if surgery, radiation, or chemo are your first stop. Because for people in this range of progression, surgery is less dangerous than chemo. And perhaps radiation to shrink the tumor first will make the tumor operable, which it currently isn’t because of what it’s right next to.

Or if it’s metastatic, maybe all three for different tumors. Excise this lymph node, radiation for the brain, etc.

↳ reply 3 — binsquare:

An it's really important to note that the trend is important too where this is the worst it will ever be.

For someone who's life expectancy after x time doubles, it also means there's more time for more treatments or innovations in treatments because of the time increase.

Top #2 — mft_:

For once, this isn’t hyperbole. Metastatic pancreatic cancer hasn’t had a meaningful new treatment in literally decades - it’s been brutal chemotherapy or slightly less brutal chemotherapy.

The new generation of KRAS inhibitors, of which daraxonrasib is just the first to make it to approval, is genuinely a practice-changing breakthrough.

It won’t cure people with metastatic disease, but it will help a lot live better lives for longer.

↳ reply 1 — matteoraso:

>Metastatic pancreatic cancer hasn’t had a meaningful new treatment in literally decades

Not true. The folfirinox chemo regimen was invented a couple of years ago, and it significantly increased the life expectancy and quality of life for terminal pancreatic cancer patients.[0]

[0]https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1011923

↳↳ reply — catoc:

“it significantly increased the life expectancy”

True. statistically it was significant.

Progression-free survival increased from 3 months to 6 months. (overall-survival increased from 7 months to 11 months).

Both statistically significant, and at the cost of increased toxicity during those additional 3 to 4 months of “’significantly’ increased life expectancy”

↳↳↳ reply — catoc:

I don’t get why this is down-voted.

To decide whether a survival of 3 to 4 months in exchange for increased toxicity (decreased quality of life during those few remaining months)

is “significant” is a very nuanced decision between the patient and their physician.

↳ reply 2 — schleck8:

> It won’t cure people with metastatic disease, but it will help a lot live better lives for longer.

Cancer is a problem that can be solved, and it needs to be solved asap. Cancer too often gets either relegated to "Actually, statistically it's very unlikely" by people who don't have it or stylized to the God of Death that unlike other illness we won't solve anytime soon. There is no time to be lost tackling with AI. Dario gets it. Had cancer himself and his father passed away from it.

Top #3 — dang:

In case others are wondering, it looks like this is a different story than this recent one:

Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50563066 - Nov 2026 (157 comments)

↳ reply 1 — catoc:

Yes, FOLFIRINOX is a combination of chemotherapeutic agents.

Which is very different from being administered an adenovirus (VRT106) that recognizes a receptor often expressed on cancer cells (MXRA8), that after ‘infecting’ the cell triggers direct oncolysis and indirect immunogenic responses.

↳ reply 2 — g-b-r:

Oh, I just assumed they were the same, incredible that there's now two very promising approaches for pancreatic cancer..!

Also — ★ tptacek:

People who pay a lot of attention to US news might know this as the therapy former senator and UF president Ben Sasse is taking.

item.title: Inkling 2 Mini
item.description: 1221 points, 237 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (thinkingmachines.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  1221 points  ·  237 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — montroser:

This is bonkers good if these benchmarks hold up in real-world scenarios. To be at the level of Qwen3.8-27B with a looped transformer model is quite the flex. They just left this note on reddit:

Hope that folks find this model more amenable to local usage - the sizing was largely informed by what folks on this subreddit ask for the most haha!

There are two particularly interesting aspects of this model for local users:

We do our training end-to-end in nvfp4, and although we haven't exhaustively benchmarked this, folks like Unsloth have noticed that our models seem to respond very well to being quantized, maintaining 90% top-1 even at at 1-bit quantization.

This model is looped, which allows more depth at the same parameter count, which we particularly notice seems helpful for coding tasks. :)

This is our first model targeted at local users, so let us know how this model is and anything you want to see out of future iterations!

https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1y1diuk/thinkin...

↳ reply 1 — nico:

> This is bonkers good if these benchmarks hold up in real-world scenarios

I think we’re going to start seeing a lot more of these types of advances, especially on smaller models

I’ve been able to graft reasoning and math problem solving into a small, locally trained model with 6.5M params. And I’ve also been able to add abilities or improve them by “growing” the model to 8.5M params (this usually means redistributing the weights in a slightly different network size, then finetune the new size)

The model is so small that I can sometimes run dozens of experiments per day. There are a lot of papers and new models coming out. A lot of the stuff they are doing at 100B-1T still works at smaller scale (usually not the scaling inference-related optimizations, but rather things like weight programming, or a “looped” architecture). It’s a lot of fun to run at home on my laptop

I imagine bigger labs with bigger budgets (more GPUs) are mostly focused on 20B-1T+ models. But there’s a lot to explore in local “home models”

↳↳ reply — 18al:

can you expand more on this? 8.5M is incredibly small, how'd you get it to the point of being able to graft reasoning and math problem solving?

i'd wanted to see if an under 100M model can perform reasonably well at word math, like GSM8k. under 10M sounds bonkers.

↳ reply 2 — ycui7:

why do people need to even quantize this model? it is already in nvfp4.

↳ reply 3 — Jackson__:

To beat a 27B model with a new architecture and 26.7B parameters, 3.5 months after said 27B model was released is not quite the flex you make it out to be.

Top #2 — hedgehog:

Seems pretty promising in a few quick coding tests. 27 tokens/s decode on Ryzen 395 and llama.cpp Vulkan. Besides the obvious unmerged PRs (32694, 32657, 32429, 32704) you'll want below tiny patch for about 30% speed boost.

Also, if anyone from the team is reading, if you have access for researchers I'd be interested in doing some higher volume tests & harness tuning than I have hardware for personally.

    --- a/src/llama-graph.cpp
    +++ b/src/llama-graph.cpp
    @@ -2670,10 +2670,12 @@ ggml_tensor \* llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn(
                         const float beta = hparams.situ_beta;
                         const float lb   = hparams.situ_linear_beta;

    -                    ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, cur, 1.0f/beta)), beta);
    +                    // gate/up are strided views of the fused gate_up output; ggml-vulkan's SCALE
    +                    // needs a contiguous src, so without the cont both scales fall back to the CPU
    +                    ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, cur), 1.0f/beta)), beta);
                         act = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, ggml_sigmoid(ctx0, cur));
                         if (lb > 0.0f) {
    -                        up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, up, 1.0f/lb)), lb);
    +                        up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, up), 1.0f/lb)), lb);
                         }
                         cur = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, up);
                         cb(cur, "ffn_moe_situ", il);

↳ reply 1 — porkloin:

Tested on a 7900xtx, I got a similar (~35%) improvement. Thanks for sharing!

↳ reply 2 — simfoo:

Tried it on my 9070XT and got 58% improvement (22.4 -> 35.5 tok/s). Nice!

Top #3 — ramshanker:

I am getting Stable Diffusion level of breakthrough vibe here. And such looped transformer SMALL models are best suited to embed directly into silicon/transistor. So you get better than ASIC performance by just looping over the hard-coded silicon. Just like we had a breakthrough with "deep" neural network, soon we may have something similar with "deep" loop over the same set of weights. Imaging transistor level looping 128 times. Extreme power efficient, and god knows what level of intelligence is achievable. I could very well foresee purchasing USB Intelligence Devices with some standardised driver protocol. You just buy one off Amazon, throw away the old one and get an Intelligence Upgrade.

Also — ★ simonw:

Pelicans aren't terrible (for the model size): https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=ht...

Top #3 — terabytest:

Even though I’m also feeling the somber mood, I’m not able to feel this change as a loss. Long term, it will probably lead to more discovery rather than less.

The worry that I have, and I haven’t seen this talked about enough, is that humanity will stop understanding how things actually work. If we delegate all scientific work to the machine, we’re not incentivized to actually understand why things are the way they are. Those who spend their time intimately studying processes and phenomena will consequently be the ones that contribute the least to progress because their work will inherently be slower and limited by their own mind’s throughput.

Losing our knowledge of how things work can be truly catastrophic and set us back heavily (or possibly end civilization) if for some reason AI stops working or goes out of our control.

↳↳↳ reply — beej71:

I've had this exact thought. Another way to phrase it is with the question: how fucked are we if LLMs evaporate today?

Today the answer is that we'd make it fine. Enough people have enough knowledge. 10 years from now? Not so sure. And 20 years is looking grim.

Also — aaron_m04:

We don't have to resign ourselves to this. We can use every means in our power to stop "AI".

↳ reply — ★ simonw:

What does that look like to you?

↳↳ reply — NateEag:

1. Government bans on training runs and owning large numbers of GPUs, enforced by imprisonment and suspension of access to computer hardware (much as happens to people caught violating computer security laws now).

2. Complete dismantling of the existing AI companies, again enforced by governments, on the grounds that every one of these companies is necessarily doing work that is ruining human societies at breakneck speeds. There is no fundamental right to make money by creating antisocial, dangerous, untrustworthy tools, however pragmatically useful they may be for removing programmers and mathematicians from the workforce.

3. Developing social norms that AI systems are long-term and big-picture very bad for humans in every respect, and that developing or using them is a betrayal of your family, friends, and the entire species. It may be fun to generate a lot of code, but the tradeoffs are brutally savage, and it's very much the "defect" choice, IMO.

4. Naming and shaming people who train AIs or use them.

5. Refusing to surrender our minds and capacity for independent thought to AI systems. Don't use them for any purposes at all.

None of this is impossible - just brutally difficult. The hardest part is getting governments to coordinate a shutdown of the technology and enforcing hard limits on GPU ownership and usage. I'm not going to say that's straightforward, but it's also not known to be impossible.

I'm not entirely sure these are actually good ideas, and restraining people's freedom disconcerts me deeply, but society is necessarily a trade-off between complete individual freedom and cooperative benefits for everyone. We don't usually let individual people own rocket launchers or heavy machine guns, and in many ways these are more dangerous.

As someone whose employers have compelled me to use Claude daily, I can see the negative impacts these systems are having up close, and I feel guilty every day for feeding the Beast.

Top #1 — mjdiloreto:

> DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone.

I think this is an enormous mistake, and it will completely stop me from using this project. Being emacs compatible software would give this project a shared base of decades of composable interoperable software, and he ditched it. Now DreamCoder is completely indistinguishable from any other vibe coded bullshit IDE.

If the author is lurking, I implore you to re-port DreamCoder back to emacs. I share a similar vision, but I took another approach.

The problem is not emacs itself (one could simply customize emacs to be more palatable), but distribution. If emacs was web software, then it _would_ be "for everyone". That's why I built emacswasm (https://codeberg.org/emacswasm/, https://emacswasm.org) - it's also vibe coded bullshit, but it does port the emacs lisp interpreter and PTY interface to Web assembly, and lets Emacs lisp call JavaScript synchronously, and lets JavaScript call emacs lisp asynchronously.

I will take a more thorough look at DreamCoder, and see if I can port a sufficient amount of features myself, because "an emacs that edits itself with AI better than I ever could manually" is my absolute dream.

↳ reply 1 — mickeyp:

It will not run in Emacs. Emacs is great, but it's fundamentally unsuited, today, in its current shape -- and by Emacs I mean GNU Emacs specifically -- to a high-fidelity, asynchronous and highly parallel agent workflow engine.

I wish it did fit the mould --- it does not. Not for what I want.

By all means avail yourself of DreamCoder's features and port them yourself though.

↳ reply 2 — torben-friis:

↳ reply 3 — fock:

(Linux is burning already and all the people renting us computers have very much decided to stoke the fire to support their case of monopolizing compute)

Top #2 — everforward:

It's interesting (and probably correct) how much this focuses on the UI.

I also looked (/am looking) at Lisp and AI, but I went with Clojure and zero-ed in on the REPL driven development. The high level idea is that a session maps to a namespace in Clojure. When you create a new session, it makes a new namespace, injects tools that are bound to that session into it, and then swaps you into that namespace. So I can do something like:

    (new!)
    (prompt! "Write me a script that does ....")
The agent configuration, tools it has, etc, etc are all bound to the namespace so you can drop a tool or change the model just for the session.

The agent also has a tool (that I've tried to encourage it to use almost exclusively) to execute code in the session's namespace (via nREPL, so same JVM as yours is connected to), so you have full access to any variables it declares, functions it makes, etc.

The idea was to be able to work collaboratively with the agent. I can e.g. load API data into a variable, point the agent at the variable, and it does stuff. It's also capable of modifying its own code. I semi-routinely poke it by asking it to add features to the harness and then use them ("add support for subagents in this workspace, and then invoke a separate agent to handle each of these tasks"). I've also had it add support for a new inference provider, swap the session to that provider and then start doing some other task.

It's very neat, and it's wildly insecure. E.g. prompt injection could theoretically make the LLM change itself to hide messages from you, there's nothing to prevent that. I'm actually not sure how you'd even go about trying to secure that, which is why it's probably a terrible idea. Fun, though.

↳ reply — maxwelljoslyn:

> The high level idea is that a session maps to a namespace in Clojure. When you create a new session, it makes a new namespace, injects tools that are bound to that session into it, and then swaps you into that namespace.

Oh, that's a fascinating idea. Well done.

Top #3 — spockz:

I just read the whole announcement and boy I wish more text was written like this. Full of history, facts, and reasoning. Beautifully written. (I recognise it is a tad long of you just want to get cracking with it.) A very nice refresher in this age.

I’ll be trying it out soon. Hopefully it does sandboxing and dealing with antigravity and codex well.

item.title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
item.description: 326 points, 298 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (scottaaronson.blog)

→ HN comments  ·  326 points  ·  298 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — Mikhail_Edoshin:

There's a book, "Impro", about a theatric studio that practiced improvised sketches. One thing they struggled with was a normal conversation. People have them all the time yet somehow artists could not find the right approach.

One day the head of the studio (the book author) had an insight. She asked the actors to drive the conversation so that they always bump the status of themselves or the other party in any direction, but only a little.

This did the magic. Not only the actors understood her perfectly, the conversation started to flow and could go endlessly while staying amusing and captivating for spectators. (Look up the book for examples.)

After they discovered that secret they started seeing the pattern (status games) everywhere up to the point they asked themselves whether there is anything else in human communication.

This was a British studio, the sketches were mostly comedy.

↳ reply 1 — dgan:

i have read your comment in full, multiple times, and I still don't understand what you re saying. > that they always bump the status of themselves or the other party in any direction.

what? English non native so that might be the reason

↳↳ reply — armchairhacker:

Every point they add makes themselves or allies look better (sometimes just more interesting, sometimes more humble) or their enemies look worse. Usually themselves better, at least me; it’s inevitable, even explaining this I notice I’m doing it.

The key for the improv actors is doing it with intention. To decide “what is the next thing I should say in this conversation” they think “how do I make my fictional self look better, or my fictional conversational partner look worse, to the audience”? And that gets them to natural-sounding phrases.

↳↳↳ reply — pseidemann:

Is that some fundamental behavior of humans confirmed by psychology? I've never heard of this before and most people I encounter don't do this. Of course there is selfishness and altruism, but it seems this is referring to something else?

↳ reply 2 — RhysU:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impro:_Improvisation_and_the_T... is an interesting, and at times strange, read.

↳ reply 3 — xg15:

I like how the book author bumped their own status with that anecdote as well...

(I'd still like to see some concrete examples here)

Top #2 — esjeon:

Lean + Stochastic predictor = Brute-force theorem solver

P.S: AlphaGo was pretty much the same in the spirit btw.

Top #3 — sc077y:

If this isn't intelligence, then I don't know what is

↳ reply — threatripper:

Maybe we don't need real intelligence or consciousness to be effective.

↳↳ reply — pseidemann:

Nobody knows what intelligence actually is. Psychology and neuroscience have no answer, and especially not computer science.

↳↳↳ reply — morpheos137:

Intelligence like consciousness is a word to describe patterns of processes tending to optimize toward some goal set under the constraints of environment and with sensory feedback. Humans goal is to reproduce. Llms goal is to predict best next token. Human feedback is sensory mediated. Llm feedback is prompting on outputs including from tools such as lean. If RH was provable it is not surprising either such system could prove it in principle. If a sound proof required an intricate path or vast contextual memory to assemble it is not surprising a machine proved it before a human. However I don't think this is generalizable. I don't think intelligence is a scalar in that the proof shows the machine is more intelligent than the human. Rather it is qualitative. The machine was structured so that the path was attainable to it. This is intelligence in the particular case but not general intelligence if such a thing exists. Now what would point more toward general intelligence is a machine that can compress proofs or truths better than humans. If we start seeing short proofs of FLT or RH then that will be interesting. I am skeptical with the current technology. The tendency of LLMs seems to be to explode complexity not condense things to essential elements or minimal description lengths.
