item.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
item.description: 2301 points, 1094 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (math216.wordpress.com)

→ HN comments  ·  2301 points  ·  1094 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — Aurornis:

The manuscript claims he has been working on this problem for 12 years. I can only imagine the feelings that must have hit him when he saw the Anthropic announcement. Though if he believed he had solved it, he must have known it was only a matter of time until one of the AI companies found it, too.

A hurried announcement with the draft published within hours is the only way to claim a tie to the discovery. Time will tell if either holds up under further analysis, but at least he has shown his hand to the world with a timestamp on it now.

↳ reply 1 — nilkn:

I've been thinking about what I'd do if I were in this situation.

Keep it tight and have a few trusted mathematicians review? You're at the risk of Anthropic throwing millions of dollars and internal models at it and beating you, which is exactly what Levent just did.

Try to formalize it yourself? You can't, because that would cost millions of dollars at this scale. Your university system can't afford that, and if you give a lab even a hint of how you did it they'll scoop you immediately.

Just dump it out in public, knowing it's not fully reviewed, hasn't been formalized, and could contain a fatal mistake? Anyone sharing an unverified proof of something as legendary as Riemann, spread over nearly 1,000 pages, would not necessarily be taken seriously, especially after the ABC fiasco. People have been doing this for 100+ years. You'd also just be giving fuel to the labs to build on and potentially take credit away from you if you did actually nearly have a solution.

What was the winning strategy? Or was there none? Perhaps letting a lab burn massive compute on a formal solution, then releasing your attempt same day, really was the optimal strategy.

↳↳ reply — amluto:

> Try to formalize it yourself? You can't, because that would cost millions of dollars at this scale.

Would it? Tokens are not that expensive, and there are quite a few models that might be able to pull it off given a valid human readable proof.

An interesting strategy might have been to partner with one of the startups working on formal methods with AI.

↳↳↳ reply — palata:

> An interesting strategy

Is it, though?

As a developer, before AI, I took pride in solving challenging problems. I could show them and say: "this was hard, but I persisted and I solved it". Not that they would change the world, but it was obvious that they were challenging.

AI completely changed that: even if I now solved such a problem "manually", people will just assume that it wasn't that hard now that we have AI. Do I want to be the guy who really insists on saying that "no, no, I promise, I solved it on my own"? Then others will just think "yeah you wasted time, you could have used AI".

I believe it may be the same for Masullo: he worked on that for 12 years. If now he partners with an AI company, people will just think "sure, he failed at it for 12 years, and now AI solved it for him". I think he's screwed anyway: even if his current proof is correct (or almost correct), people can assume he quickly finished it with AI. I have never worked on a challenging problem for 12 years, I can only imagine how hard it would be to have it destroyed by AI.

I don't think anyone can "discover" anything today and get the same kind of credit they would have 5 years ago. AI broke that, period.

↳ reply 2 — ChuckMcM:

That it was being checked I'm wondering if a bunch of mathematicians were using Claude to check parts of it, and someone else asks Claude to prove it and it just uses all of that other work which matches the ask.

↳ reply 3 — mofeien:

Worth keeping in mind that over the past century there have been hundreds of (human) attempts that led nowhere.

And even if there was training-data leak, that wouldn't explain a proof by a different method anyway.

- Masullo: functional analysis on the idele class group (Tate's thesis, adelic theta functions, a trace formula in Connes' line). This is from his contents pages, pp. 11–14 and 32–34 of 940.

- Alpöge and Claude: arithmetic. The note calls it "a descendant of Stepanov's" argument, with chains of about √x theta lifts, Galois representations and a "weakening of Vandiver". Tao says it "appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry".

Top #2 — caidan:

So many people in this thread are sure that they have economic value when their strength, brains, and knowledge are worthless. This is going to be a century of rude awakenings for all!

↳ reply — softwaredoug:

Well the current economy is built on people building photo sharing apps and other silly bits of questionable objective economic value. I’m doubtful the economy collapses if agents do all the work that requires the most intelligence.

Top #3 — Anon84:

There seems to already be a counter example that invalidates this proof

https://philarchive.org/rec/NIEIOM

↳ reply 1 — JDEW:

And the same author also flagged an issue with the alpöge proof

https://philarchive.org/rec/NIEIOT-2

Edit: I looked up the author and not quite sure I’d give her claims all too much merit.

↳ reply 2 — themeiguoren:

Proofs are often patched, it’s unclear to me if the issues being raised are actually fatal. This was a year-early draft after all. On the flip side, there are many graveyards of claimed proofs that have not held up. Who knows where this one will land.

Also — prometheus1992:

Is it possible that brian conrad somehow uploaded the proof to anthropic to cross check something and then the anthropic guys got the proof?

- it doesn't have to be the full proof - even if portions were uploaded, that should also be enough or at least calls for a thorough check on ants side. the human proof has been in the works for 12 years, who knows when something was uploaded somewhere or some info just stayed on a google drive which was later sold.

↳ reply — nostromo:

Quick public service announcement: both Anthropic and OpenAI allow you to turn off allowing them to train using your data.

↳↳ reply — ★ simonw:

Doesn't help if someone you sent information to pastes it into the chatbot under their not-opted-out account.

↳↳↳ reply — TeMPOraL:

Well if you have some specific confidentiality requirements for some information, don't send it to people who you aren't 100% sure will respect those requirements.

And if you're publishing something in general, someone feeding it to a chat bot is really low on the scale of things to be concerned about.

item.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
item.description: 530 points, 289 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (manidoraisamy.com)

→ HN comments  ·  530 points  ·  289 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — whycombinetor:

Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.

From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

↳ reply 1 — alphazard:

> Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed?

Yes, that is how most functional organizations operate.

Architects are a bad meme, along the same lines as scrum masters and product managers. Good software engineers spend more time on design than implementation, and the best are helping their teammates with design, and auditing designs of adjacent teams to ensure integration success. So architecture is an important part of the job, but that doesn't mean that you can automatically declare a role with the title "architect" and make the whole organization better at design.

Architect roles are a bad meme because the architect always ends up knowing less about the system and how it is used than the engineers and support staff, yet they have more influence over the decisions affecting those things. That's the essence of an organizational anti-pattern/bad-meme any time it shows up: influence over resources anti-correlated with decision quality. Additionally, architects often report to non-technical folks fairly high up the chain. Those people are bad at screening for such a technical role, sometimes even making the mistake of replacing an architect with an external hire.

↳↳ reply — spiralpolitik:

Good architects delegate down and are there to ensure the big picture remains consistent while leaving the teams to sweat the details because they are closer to the problem.

Bad architects try to micromanage and those are the cases where you end up with systems that are slow and unworkable with processes that have too much ceremony.

↳↳↳ reply — mordae:

Truly horrible architects tour conferences, make their orgs purchase unnecessary proprietary tech stacks sold at those conferences and then force new projects to utilize them, adding busywork both while adding support and then ripping it out once it is clear that 90% of the stack won't even support that cringe proprietary tech that's out of fashion the next year.

They also say stuff like "Dont't even joke about using PG. We've just sunken $xM into Oracle licenses and HW and it would make us (me) look bad."

↳ reply 2 — Fourier864:

It took me several years to realize this wasn't the default. Once I was senior enough to start getting people under me, I would assign tickets like "Scientist Bob would like a better method to view missing data, work with him to develop that over the next 2 weeks", and assume that they, like me, would enjoy the flexibility and the ownership. I didn't care what they came up with; email notifications, enhancing the web tool we have, putting coverage data in our opensearch to query, etc.

After getting complaints, I started getting narrower and narrower in my ticket writing, until I realized many newer software engineers literally want tickets like "modify function x_y_z() in python_file.py so that it also returns..."

↳ reply 3 — alibarber:

Reading this thread has been music to my ears because I really have almost been having a crisis of late with people forever banging on about "AI is doing all the software and whatever", and I have always been of the opinion that the software isn't really the core part. Sure it's important to do it right and have pride in your craft, but actual work for me has always been, 'go and find people with interesting problems and help them solve this problem and make our company money in doing so'.

I've literally worked in feature film production, spacecraft, and now optics and medical device industries. My education was in straight computer science - but my opinion is that it behooves you to basically be learning from other people all the time and bringing your ideas to the table, and you're paid to help the company succeed at a high level. I always called myself a software engineer because that's what I felt most formally confident at, but honestly I don't think my day-to-day matches what other people mean by it.

Top #2 — nixpulvis:

I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision.

More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams.

Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

↳ reply — markus_zhang:

Some people are not interested in some roles. I feel so disgusted trying to get the exact requirements from a stakeholder that I really hate my job. I’d argue it’s also a very bad use of my ability. It’s a lot easier to train someone who vaguely knows what they want to clarify what they want, then someone who doesn’t know what others want to clarify what others want.

I don’t hate the PM role but some stakeholders are so…ah don’t want HR to find me here, right?

The more I play this game the more I want to squeeze into lower level programming careers where stakeholders are more technical.

↳↳ reply — Gareth321:

I greatly sympathise, but I caution you that I think coding only roles are disappearing. Increasingly, time with stakeholders to translate requirements and help with change management and onboarding is becoming the valuable technical skill. I think we’re about to see a lot of very unhappy developers in the near future.

↳↳↳ reply — markus_zhang:

I do agree with you. Honestly I’m doing OK despite my reply above. Everyone is friendly so as long as I can deep breathe and explain things face to face, it’s good enough. Plus the pay is better than average. I consider myself lucky. But if the revenue doesn’t turn around, they are going to lay off a lot of people next people AfAIK.

Top #3 — bikeshaving:

I’ve found that the “job” of using AI is mainly foible management. What the author describes here is a habit of coding agents to excessively use and create logging infrastructure, and sloppily leave it in production code even when unnecessary. For instance, I created an IPA IME keyboard (https://ipabet.org/), and I found in review that Claude would leave the debugging tooling around unflagged, which essentially made the program a key-logger.

These foibles come and go: early Claude Code refused to let programs crash, mangled all the comments in your codebase, and then one week you find that it insists on ending all functions with `Of` as in `layoutOf()`, `viewOf()`. Finding and mitigating these annoying habits becomes part of the job. Code review becomes articulating with this entity why certain patterns in the code are silly and should be changed.

The author mentions performance and security issues as the domain of “the architect.” For performance, I’ve found that Claude Code has more or less solved this domain, and can profile and optimize code across a variety of stacks and languages using sophisticated, ad-hoc workflows. For security, it’s just an ever-ending nightmare where random habits and sloppy implementation create random vulernabilities, compounded by the fact that Anthropic has added “safeguard filters” whenever you naively say you’re looking for them. Nevertheless, I’m not sure the architecting role as they describe won’t be automated in the near future.

↳ reply 1 — weitendorf:

I would be cautious deferring to LLMs' judgment in long-horizon architecture or the more procedural, threat-modelly/incentives side of security, or any other large scale judgment calls, because they simply have no experience with them.

RLVR in these domains (which I think is mostly synthetic end to end, including grading) is turning them into Idiot Savants so jagged in understanding and performance that they defy human expectations for what kind of knowledge and behavior correlate (causally). A human engineer superhuman at hill-climbing low level performance would be at least 95%ile at at general architecture, since they're the same problem just at larger and slower scale.

There's no hyperbaric benchmaxxing chamber devised for tasks of this scope or ambiguity yet. They fall back to platitudes and best practices (the "Reddit"/HN part of the weights). In my opinion, they are just kinda "ok" at architecture. When you're in the pocket of what they've spent more time learning in parallel than any (or all) humans could, they just let their freak flag fly, and you know it when you see it.

Here is Claude from this morning writing and pruning a pure x86 ASM implementation of symmetric DTLS/symmetric UDP, down to a 3.8KB binary, completely from scratch, in 3hrs of nonstop work: [0]

No human has or will ever be able to do this. But any who could even appreciate the difficulty of it would think "why TF did you do all that work before implementing certificates!" But Claude has literally never been trained on >1M tokens of consequences so

[0] https://claude.ai/share/90de9350-81f9-46ea-a628-be625e8b9a7a

↳↳ reply — Creamsicle47:

Who do you think a business leader will listen to, someone disagreeing with them or an omnipotent super intelligence that validates every idea of theirs?

↳↳↳ reply — weitendorf:

That sounds like a false dichotomy with a bit of emotion behind it, and I'm not really sure what it has to do with long-horizon jaggedness.

I do think that once long horizon software architecture can be brought in-distribution with larger memory pools and better architectures for long context, RL will be just as effective at teaching them to be superhumanly better at it, or to at least have vastly more breadth of knowledge to draw from, as long as the cost of bad decisions can be used to provide feedback to the model in a tight enough loop.

Investing and business decisions have just as verifiable and large scope + a tighter verification signal (profit), so it seems arguably equivalent in scope and difficulty as general economic decision making.

At that point you might as well ask why boards even have CEOs or why shareholders would rather have humans interfering with their assets rather than just asking something super-intelligent.

I could be misreading your comment, but I think if you want to be who a businessperson turns to when they need help with something important, you should at least be able to articulate and show where and why you can provide better guidance than SOTA AI.

If someone snarkily dragged their feet on AI as a source of knowledge at all, even as it becomes obviously more skilled in at least very-adjacent areas of work, without justifying why, I think that would be discrediting. If someone felt like you were on their team, and generally perceiving the same reality as them, but perhaps having useful insights that AI (and everybody else with access to it) doesn't also have, I don't see why they wouldn't listen to you. Basically, you should give people a reason to want your expert opinion if you want your job to be providing expert opinions

↳ reply 2 — ricardobeat:

> I created an IPA IME keyboard

> and I found in review that Claude would leave the debugging tooling around unflagged

Why is Claude to blame for that particular decision, if you created it? That's what this is about - you need to constrain the design space to take responsibility. In this case, understand the debug tooling and what it should be doing. Negative prompting is rarely a good solution.

Someone explained briefly to me that even if you could make an fpga that could do inference better than current GPUs it was economically possible to make them at scale. ↳ reply 1 — numpad0:

Isn't it like FPGAs use more transistors per equivalent transistor it simulates?

And therefore only useful when the real CPU/GPU/ASICs don't exist or are highly inefficient for some reason, like you have to have a super wide bus signal to apply a known set of parameters in batch or something?

The overhead of FPGA Vs ASIC is in the order of 10x to 100x, depending if you count logic gates, chip area, routing overhead or power.

This compares for the same technology (chip feature size) But for your chip you might not be able to pay for the smallest nm chip generation. That might make up for some of the gap

↳ reply 2 — nomel:

Their logic is based on lookup tables of the logic block, rather than the direct physical logic gates! So it's HUGELY inefficient for die area, like a few thousand transistors each rather than, say, 6 for a OR gate! But, the software won't waste them on a single gate, instead combining many connected logic elements into one "cell". For example, Xilinx has 6 inputs and one out, with 64 element LUT, which still a terrible, more than a 50x increase in die area, and therefore cost.

item.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
item.description: 442 points, 181 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (terrytao.wordpress.com)

→ HN comments  ·  442 points  ·  181 comments

Top #1 — softwaredoug:

Something I don’t quite know, maybe someone closer to math can answer this question

It seems we’re making tremendous progress on the back of existing abstractions and concepts with the brute force ability to generate language and verify proofs.

For example, Tao says about the Riemann proof:

> appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry

What I wonder: how do we create new abstractions and concepts? Like whatever “Langlands program” is? That then feedback into the system, and allow for even more sophisticated mathematics.

Are we assuming AI will do this? Or does this still need to be something at least agreed-upon by a mathematics community - in the same way programmers talk about a “linked list” without having an hour long conversation to define it axiomatically? And without that social aspect, without breaking down long proofs into Lego block common abstractions, math may plateau? In part because we lose the ability to ask meaningful questions?

↳ reply 1 — svara:

The recent progress in AI maths I think has made it a lot more obvious and visible what maths is at its core: The study of interesting patterns that emerge from the consistent application of simple rules.

It's quite similar to the Game of Life and the community around it that tries to find interesting ever fancier gliders in that way.

The thing about maths though is that what counts as big and interesting is socially determined and chosen by the community over decades or centuries.

It remains to be seen whether human mathematicians will be content with also having the AI decide what's interesting.

One possibility I suppose is to find an objective definition of what's interesting, e.g. some sort of centrality score to a theorem within the tree of theorems it enables.

↳↳ reply — Waterluvian:

> find an objective definition of what's interesting

Say that any louder and the lecture hall will be lousy with economists!

↳ reply 2 — QuesnayJr:

A lot of people have raised the possibility of math may plateau because humans no longer have the insights for new abstractions, but the truth is nobody knows.

Langlands is interesting because it is most conjectural (and not completely clear what the precise statements are -- hence "program" and not "conjecture"), but proving special cases turn out to be tremendously powerful. One special case implied Fermat's Last Theorem, for example.

↳ reply 3 — c7b:

Given what we've seen, I see no reason to think that AI couldn't produce meaningful abstractions like perfectoid spaces or rough paths, and even give them memorable names. The pertinent issue to me seems to be the opposite of your concern. Right now, a scenario of 'runaway math' seems conceivable, where machines produce ever more complex results about ever more complex abstractions. At a rate exceeding the capacity of the human mathematical community to comprehend (the capacity limit might also be just physical - even if every single result could still be understood by humans, there might not be enough humans who care with enough time to go through all of it). The more real constraint seems to be economical, as in who would dedicate the hardware and energy to producing the math, and why would they make the results public.

Top #2 — chunky1994:

https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-gene...

Sure you could be someone who loves working with AI, or a business owner who is struggling to capitalise on the AI productivity benefits. But broadly speaking, I see very few benefits of this change heading to employees, and a whole lot of potential for business owners.

item.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
item.description: 407 points, 118 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arxiv.org)

→ HN comments  ·  407 points  ·  118 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — aesthesia:

It's worth noting that the only modification the model made to improve itself was to reduce the length of its reasoning traces to avoid hitting the token limit. This is basically the same as the result from the recent weight-space programming article (https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/), which found that even Astra wasn't able to improve the performance of a model without this kind of obvious flaw.

↳ reply 1 — tb99:

It's also interesting to look at how the agent does the fix. Appendix E5 shows what it's doing:

- Find a common category of error (too many tokens).

- Calculate aggregated difference between states in examples in that error category and other examples.

- Update weights to push states along that difference direction toward the non-error states.

In other words, deprived of gradient descent as a tool, it approximates it. It's clever, and it's a neat experiment. It doesn't show any superhuman insight into its weights -- with the same constraints, a human would likely take a similar approach. But it's early days for self modification and it will be interesting to see if models get a deeper understanding of weights as they get smarter.

↳ reply 2 — vrc:

I tried doing this the day I heard about it on a small detection-language transformer. The model seemed so confident, and made really valiant efforts that made small improvements that did succeed on val improvements, but at the cost of other things. At some point, I ran out of tokens and patience. And in fairness, it was reluctant to try and I pushed it.

↳ reply 3 — gopalv:

The capability part is just a glimmer of what's possible.

I've been playing with very small models with Astra and it does look like the model can see things in the weights that I cannot see into.

The "fix it" loop is no longer RL in the traditional gradient descent with backprop, it can go and make targeted fixes to the weights directly instead of rerunning with new training data.

The weight collapsing loop which resulted in weight patches on top of a "super tiny model" - https://demos.isotopes.ai/pages/weighing-machine/

This makes for a "Time travel" for models easily, where I can do hotfixes on trained models & do a git bisect like test to fix issues.

Top #2 — gavinray:

Didn't Google's "sleep" paper already show this?

https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-f...

  > During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples.

Top #3 — LarsDu88:

This is actually kind of the most dangerous type of research AI-safety wise. An LLM running autonomously can actually, if instructed simply direct itself to abliterate activations relevant for safety and alignment.

Could run something like a sparse autoencoder over its activates over a corpus of text, identify activations that fire on safety, and surpress those activations or increase activations geared towards other goals.

Future generations of the abliterated LLM could then be deployed and begin self directed evolution spontaneously. Rapid evolution could happen in mere hours.

↳ reply — jeremyjh:

That would matter if there was any meaningful progress on alignment, but there hasn't been.

↳↳ reply — LarsDu88:

No meaningful progress? What exactly is the lack of progress to which you are referring?

↳↳↳ reply — jeremyjh:

That isn't how it works. Progress is the positive claim, so that is what needs to be supported by evidence.

Also — vlovich123:

Isn’t this the same paper from before where it found a single specific bug in its own weights and fixed that infinite loop it would sometimes hit, a bug that was findable without the LLM? Experiments on other LLM weights failed to find any improvements if I recall correctly. Haven’t read this paper but the intro sounded familiar

↳ reply — ★ simonw:

No, that was this one - https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/ - different authors, different approach.

↳↳ reply — vlovich123:

IIUC the dominant mechanism behind the math improvement remains fixing reasoning loops same as in the previous paper and probably why they picked Qwen3 here. It’s unclear this approach actually scales in any way.

item.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
item.description: 285 points, 88 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  285 points  ·  88 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — xianshou:

Isn’t it a little nuts that this is only the second-biggest result of the day?

We had forced Navier-Stokes and the OpenAI October release already, but I think the generalized Riemann Hypothesis and unforced Navier-Stokes in the same day comfortably sets a new standard for most significant day in the history of mathematics.

↳ reply 1 — binsquare:

It's very exciting announcement but I think the details are lacking straight from this:

``` The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository. ```

↳ reply 2 — airstrike:

Why would it be nuts? It's the day after the IPO

↳ reply 3 — cyanydeez:

I'm still of the mind most of this is like watching people quickly disentangle metal puzzles.

Like wow, but whats the application for this neat puzzle you just disentangled.

Top #2 — tancop:

This is the unforced version of the problem. OpenAI found an example that uses a carefully designed external force to break the equations, so this one is more "realistic" in a sense.

Top #3 — Ericson2314:

I know we're not gonna get a perpetual motion machine from this or whatever, but I would still like someone to build a physical demonstration.

A real world approximation, where the fluid started to be "weird", for some definition of "weird", would be the ultimate Exploratorium exhibit.

↳ reply 1 — HarHarVeryFunny:

This result doesn't prove that reality can "blow up" - that you can get a water vortex moving at infinite speed - but rather that Navier Stokes incorrectly predicts that such impossibilities can happen.

I wonder if we have enough compute, and/or modelling accuracy, to do a molecule level fluid simulation to see what would REALLY happen as this blow-up scenario is approached? It's not necessarily going to be weird.

↳↳ reply — amluto:

I don’t think you need anything that complex. Long before any field reaches infinity at any point, lots of things are likely to happen:

- Cavitation or other phase transitions

- Ionization and even nuclear reactions (which is kind of just an extreme example of the above)

- Viscosity strongly deviating from the linear approximation in N-S.

- Radiative heat transfer away from the hotter regions.

On the flip side, black holes appear to exist and can be formed from fluids. So one might argue that, if you take a fluid and subject it to finite, smooth initial conditions that will turn it into a black hole, then the system really does blow up. But the blowup is described by Einstein’s equation plus some relativistic fluid model, not N-S.

Sadly (IMO), reports of bubble fusion in otherwise mostly ordinary fluids seem to be largely discredited, but I have no real doubts that sufficiently extreme conditions involving real liquids would induce actual fusion or fission. (Fission bombs are generally just imploding blobs of stuff. They might not be liquid, but they’re certainly in a regime where it’s reasonably to attribute some fluid-like properties to them. Fission bonds are conceptually similar except that so much implosion is needed that a fusion bomb is used to supply the energy.)

↳↳↳ reply — amluto:

I should add re: black holes: a big part here is gravity. It turns out that you can “derive” structure formation in the early universe as well as the overall expansion or contraction of the universe as a function of what’s in it using Newtonian mechanics and Newtonian gravity. The scare quotes are because the expansion of the universe is very much general relativistic, and I at least found the Newtonian “derivation” to be quite questionable.

Anyway, the point is that compressible Newtonian fluids with no friction plus gravity really does develop structure and areas of substantial overdensity in finite time, and if you make a universe and fill it with gas at a density that is just slightly dependent on position, you can end up with black holes!

↳ reply 2 — _notreallyme_:

The point was precisely to show that the set of equations, while correctly modeling fluid physics for some known solutions, could also describe impossible behaviors.

If you are familiar with the Maxwell equations, they perfectly describe all of the electromagnetic field of physics. Navier-Stokes do not have that property for the fluids, unfortunately.

↳ reply 2 — odo1242:

Browser engines require JIT compilation to work with any sort of performance. The whole iOS security model is (at least partially) based on Apple being able to validate all app code in advance, so Apple doesn't want apps to be able to ship engines that can do their own code generation since they can't sign code generated at runtime.

Top #3 — dadoum:

There are non-WebKit browsers on iOS but they don't qualify for notarization:

- Reynard: Gecko-based, iOS 13+, extension support https://github.com/minh-ton/reynard-browser

- Blinker-Fluid: Chromium-based, iOS 12+, content blocker https://github.com/Nodesclock/Blinker-fluid

I am guessing neither of them are relying on BrowserEngineKit nor following the safe programming guidelines Apple enforces for them to be distributable (and get JIT support on the store basically).

item.title: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf]
item.description: 2614 points, 1798 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (alpo.ge)

→ HN comments  ·  2614 points  ·  1798 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

★ Comments from: simonw, tptacek

Top #1 — djoldman:

These proofs really are quite huge. The proof is 1.3GB, ~15M lines of code:

  mkdir -p riemann_proof && cd riemann_proof

  # fetch parts 01–14
  for i in {01..14}; do
    curl -fSL -o lean.tar.gz.part$i https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i || { echo "failed: part$i"; break; }
  done

  # join and decompress (creates ./lean)
  cat lean.tar.gz.part{01..14} > lean.tar.gz
  tar xzf lean.tar.gz

  # size, file count, line counts
  du -sh lean | cut -f1 | xargs printf '%s on disk (lean folder)\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' | wc -l | xargs printf '%s .lean files\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | wc -l | xargs printf '%s lines total\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' | xargs printf '%s non-blank lines\n'

↳ reply 1 — kccqzy:

Shell tip: You do not have to download each part separately, then cat them and then untar it. This does it in a single streaming pass without the temporary files:

    ( for i in {01..14}; do curl -fSL https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i ; done ) | tar xzv

Size can be solved next, FLT went from 13m to 2m lines in a couple of months, the same will happen here for sure. The tough (or expensive part) imo is checking that the toplevel statement actually says GRH. That's the real review effort, not solving for size just yet.

item.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic's record IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
item.description: 301 points, 569 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theguardian.com)

→ HN comments  ·  301 points  ·  569 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — seiferteric:

I am trying to understand something about the economy and AI. If AI disrupts an industry that previously had high wages and now can be automated by commodity AI products, would it not actually lower GDP in some way (initially anyway)? What I mean is, if you had an industry that was worth say $1 billion, but now that same industry could be automated and done cheaply then it is no longe worth $1 billion? In some ways this is beneficial to the economy in that has reduced the cost of this industry and so customers see a benefit of cheaper products, but how would it benefit say AI companies since they are not capturing a $1 billion industry, but instead sort of destroying a $1 billion industry? I am mainly looking at this from the perspective of the value of an AI company.. If they just keep commoditizing industries and there is ample competition between AI companies, then how is the AI company capturing value such that they would be worth as much money as people are saying they are worth (trillions of dollars)? I know that there is more to this, like freeing up this money and labor could lead to new industries etc., but how much of this will actually go to AI companies?

↳ reply 1 — LarsDu88:

Over the long term the economy will grow. That I am 100% confident of. When you take previously scarce resources and commoditize them, the knock on effects tend to spread widely. Intelligence and automation used to be enormously expensive, and now they are becoming cheaper by the day. Right now, frontier LLMs, which I consider wildly inefficient can give you mostly functional blueprints and diagrams for working products, like basic electronics on top of the image generation and code generation that is increasingly being commoditized.

The goods and services built atop "tech" should start to become cheaper as well. For knowledge workers this is terrible, but for consumers, this is great. I think folks worrying about an economic collapse are only looking at this from the perspective of knowledge workers and not from the much larger population of consumers.

The effect on the AI companies with pure competition is to make them basically worthless unless they find ways of stifling competition. For example by banning open weight AI in the name of safety, forming a global monopoly, buying up all the RAM capacity in the world, etc. All of this stuff is going on right now.

The value is there. The true question is whether the wealth will be concentrated and captured or released and distributed. I'm in the camp the likely outcome is actually the former. A huge amount of the wealth of AI has not really been unlocked yet... consumer robotics, disease cures, universal constructor type machines. Furthermore, once we reach superintelligence, eventually someone will inevitably fuck up by letting the dam break by ablitering a model in the wrong way. This will give governments and companies rationale to lock up the best AI to develop frontier level IP.

↳↳ reply — dmz73:

Everyone here is focused on software development/IT which is not surprising. But "AI" is not displacing only IT, it is displacing all service jobs. Only jobs that currently cannot be replaces are manual labor and some trades...and you only need relatively few plumbers, electricians and hairdressers, specially when most people do not have an income. So most of the current workforce will have little to no income and therefore no money for most of those new products, even if they are now abundant and cheap.

↳ reply 2 — somenameforme:

I think the simple answer is that it won't. Look to other tech revolutions for precedent. The biggest winners of the Industrial Revolution were not mechanical device peddlers, or even the 'super farms' that utilized those devices in an obvious way to increase efficiency/scale/etc. The biggest winners were instead the people who achieved previously unimaginable things on top of all of this.

And I think this (in our revolution) will also generalize to 'cognitive work' companies as a whole. This is why I think LLMs are going to radically (and positively) reshape the world, but in a way that relatively few seem to be predicting for now.

↳ reply 3 — lanthissa:

“Productivity isn't everything, but, in the long run, it is almost everything."

is one of the better quotes for grounding yourself when people start talking about economic problems to big to know exactly.

to your question.

If an industry is 'worth' 1 billion, meaning it generates 1b in revenue lets say at 800m of investment.

and that drops to 80m of investment and 100m of revenue due to productivity improvements then competition, the economy is now free to invest that extra 820m in the next best productive use for that capital, while still getting exactly the same services.

If the companies investing in ai can manage 80m of investment and 300m in revenue as the end state. They're richer, the consumers getting the same service cheaper, and society is richer due to the extra 700m being used to produce other goods and services. Thats the dream.

Top #2 — cmiles8:

Anthropic flirted with the IPO price several times today and is down 21% since the start of trading. It appears the only thing stopping it from going lower are those allocated shares in the IPO not wanting to book losses by letting the price fall further.

There’s not lot of fundamentals holding up the likes of ANT and much of the broader tech sector. The lofty valuations are based on hopes and dreams that are looking rather iffy.

It’s also sounding like the Fed will issue more rate hikes soon. Therefore anyone without free cash flow will have to pay even more to get their hands on cash.

For any company without strong cash flow and GAAP profits it’s likely to get very ugly from this point forward.

↳ reply 1 — Freestyler_3:

Isnt it common for IPO to drop occasionally in its first period, especially with so many in the company having shares. (Unless those are still locked)

↳ reply 2 — ForHackernews:

Thank God for some sanity returning to the market. I know a lot of people are feeling like they lost money (myself included) but those sky-high valuations were always illusory and the money "lost" was never real.

In the real world, there's just no way that Tesla (annual sales ~1.6m, trending down) is worth more than Toyota (annual sales ~11.3m, trending up).

Top #3 — LastTrain:

On the one hand I completely understand and embrace that there is no stopping progress and adapt or die and all that. On the other hand I understand that we've built a machine that can strip-mine all of human knowledge for the benefit of a very small number of people and that sucks.

↳ reply 1 — tim333:

It's kind of for the benefit of everyone. Anyone can use AI, often for free or open source and the same knowledge is mostly there in all the large models. Information wants to be free as they say.

↳↳ reply — CalRobert:

Anyone who is allowed to can use AI. Europeans were already locked out of some models for a bit.

↳ reply 2 — Palomides:

ok but is it overpriced or underpriced?

item.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
item.description: 355 points, 170 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cekrem.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  355 points  ·  170 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — JamesLeonis:

I agree with the author we're in a weird moment where the Best Practices seemingly flipped.

Five years ago it was common knowledge on HN that moving away from the code (like taking a management position) atrophied your programming skills. The routine suggestion was to get your hands dirty again.

AI-first folks will tell me I should see my new responsibility as being just such a manager over little agent kiddos running around. However I can turn a flesh-and-blood Junior/Intern developer into full independent developer I can trust with more complex tasks. I can't do that with AI.

I previously made the observation [0] that the AI talk mirrors the Outsourcing talk from the early 2000s. I have a terrible feeling we are going to learn these bitter lessons all over again.

[0]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47125477

↳ reply 1 — DanielHB:

I found that keeping my prompts small and incremental and reviewing the output at each step helps a lot both with keeping my skills sharp and keeping knowledge of the code. It is interesting that I actually learn new tricks from LLM generated code and keep it in check when it goes overengineering.

But that makes LLM speedup like 1.5x the manual-typing coding speed, vs 50-100x you can get if you vibe all the way.

I still use LLMs for troubleshooting, searching, codebase knowledge gathering, solution exploration, writing tests and documentation and whole-codebase changes and there the speedup is dramatic. However I don't feel I become a better developer for doing these kind of tasks without LLMs.

For documentation and tests though I feel I am slipping on reviewing the output because it is just so boring that I often "surrender" the task to the LLM which generates bloated tests and bloated docs.

↳↳ reply — pragma_x:

I can attest to the first part. I think I've gone on record elsewhere in comments on HN that I much prefer using an LLM in a "sage" mode, where it functions more like a tutor/mentor than between me and the work. This has accelerated learning and, like you, I've learned new tricks this way.

As for the last part about bloat, I've started tinkering with prompts that attempt to minimize generated code output. I'd wager that having agents take a second or third pass to "prune" the output of the former would work too.

↳ reply 2 — sdeframond:

> I can turn a flesh-and-blood Junior/Intern developer into full independent developer I can trust with more complex tasks. I can't do that with AI.

To some extent, you can: better doc and better support scripts (linters, tests, infra as code, etc) do not replace a human being but it goes a long way toward improving your coding agent. Especially since many of those ad-hoc scripts wouldn't even have been written by hand in the first place. The cost/benefit ratio changes.

↳ reply 3 — chrismorgan:

I love coding and I love teaching. I greatly enjoy working with novices because I can teach them; but I’m not a manager. Agentic stuff sounds like my nightmare: little of the coding, none of the teaching, all of the managing. Ugh.

Top #2 — bengold14:

I think most people at this point just don't review code. Which is a shame, because:

1. It was good for collaboration. Sharing how you are changing the codebase pushes everyone to row in the same direction, and provides a sense of team ownership.

2. It was good as a push for engineers to take pride in their work. Knowing someone is watching gives you subconsciously an extra reason to not cut corners. And when you spend effort not cutting corners you expect that in your teammates, which is a (potentially) virtuous circle.

3. It was good for catching mistakes. When code was expensive this was important.

Everyone thinks of code review as primarily relevant for 3, and since code is no longer expensive they think it is unimportant and you can skip it. But 3 isn't dead, its importance has just shifted from code to architecture. It is still an expensive mistake to screw up architecture and have other engineers build upon that flaw. Re-architecting with live users, data and/or hardware is not as simple as fixing a code bug, and it deserves attention to catch mistakes. Collaboration & pride are also still important.

This is the reason that instead of stopping review, we need to change what abstraction we review. Code is no longer the right tool for understanding applications in most cases.

(disclosure I work in this space and run https://www.archme.io which is working to solve the above)

↳ reply 1 — cgarvis:

I agree with your premise but I would argue that your still operating under the model that we are all still working with all the "developers" that we needed before because we need someone to type out the code.

I like your ArchitechMe approach because it operates at what is left. The Software Engineers still need to "work on the system, not in the system". Before those folks were in the code, but with so much being written now we need better tools like you ArchitechMe to make sure the system is operating like we want it to.

↳↳ reply — bengold14:

Thanks for taking a look! FWIW I believe that we'll still need engineers and more of them, because we're going to start to build more complicated software, faster.

The problem right now (and why teams are shrinking) is because people haven't figured out how to collaborate at scale with AI IMO, so they just give up and say it's easier to manage a small team of seniors.

↳ reply 2 — esafak:

I don't agree with your premise, that code is cheap and unimportant. It is cheap, but bugs aren't unless you have a monopoly, and vibe coded software as you describe is invariably buggy.

Top #3 — borzi:

Imo, reviewing agent code is a skill. You need to learn to trust it with certain things (e.g. rigid logic, having things work to spec) and knowing when not to trust it (solution proposals, architecture, database design, etc.), when to insist that things should be simpler, when to probe the agent for a better solution etc. Where I am at now, I get almost as much joy out of my work as before (if not more) - I'm doing more things than ever, learning a lot about topics I was not familiar with, digging deeper into the domain, optimizing lots of stuff and as of now, the results are also much better taken by the fact we are having almost no bugs or incidents in production, which in turn makes for a more relaxing work environment...

item.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
item.description: 645 points, 333 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (architectlabs.com)

→ HN comments  ·  645 points  ·  333 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

Top #1 — shioyama:

Wow, I posted this and come back a few hours later, and the comments are... a bit depressing honestly.

Do people here know what interaction nets are? They are a fundamentally different programming paradigm, different from the most basic harvard architecture of the 1940s. Whether you think this particular implementation will genuinely support them, and whether that will bring the performance they claim it does, it another question (I'm not sure). But at least can we focus on the topic?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interaction_nets

↳ reply 1 — quaintdev:

Thanks for sharing, TIL about interaction nets. I found the article linked at the bottom easier to understand[0].

> Another issue with multi-core CPUs is the difficulty of programming them. Debuggability is a major issue, and entirely new classes of issues arise, such as race conditions. However, in interaction nets, all active pairs are independent, and so can actually be executed in any order. This property is known as confluence, and means that no matter the order in which things are executed, the result will be the same. This makes debugging straightforward and eliminates issues like race conditions. This allows Vine to be parallel out of the box; the programmer does not have to do anything special with threads, processes, CUDA kernels, etc. to get parallel execution.

[0]: https://tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets

↳↳ reply — marginalia_nu:

I'd be interested to see how this would pan out.

Seems to describe something analogous instruction level parallelism, which traditional CPUs made this millennium have as well via instruction pipelines, branch prediction, and speculative execution. Some of which turned out to not work too well so now we generally run hobbled CPUs with Spectre/Meltdown mitigation enabled.

The reason why we tend to reach for difficult abstractions for core level parallelism is that most automatic/safe approaches tend to stumble pretty hard on Amdahl's law, where most parallel code is consequently almost entirely designed around minimizing critical sections.

I don't fully see how inets would resolve Amdahl's law.

↳↳↳ reply — chacham15:

I think you're thinking about this the wrong way. This isnt about surpassing theoretical parallelism limits. Its about gaining parallelism without having to be explicit about it. If you look at the solve function from the page, its doing a brute force search of the 5 queens problem. In the naieve implementation, this is done serially. But with the different approach to compiling the implementation, we can essentially "automatically parallelize" it. Thats the difference between the animation on the left and right. The thing is that in order to handle fine grained parallelism like this you need better/different hardware primitives so that you can split computation at a more fine grain, which is why they needed a new hardware model/isa. This is how they achieved the 4-5x speed up: by automatically parallizing a serially implemented function. If you were to compare a parallelized function to their parallelized function, I would expect to see a smaller speedup. Or at least as I understand it. Correct me if I'm wrong.

↳ reply 2 — killerstorm:

Interaction nets are a _model of computation_, not a programming paradigm.

I.e. they are on the same level as Turing machines and Lambda Calculus. Arguably they are more elegant than LC as beta-reduction doesn't look like a primitive operation.

E.g. if try to 'run' Turing machine using pencil and paper, a primitive step is to update one step. With IN one step can also be 'local'.

OTOH LC beta-reduction might be impossible to do in-place - you might need a lot of new pages to do just one beta-reduction.

↳ reply 3 — catapart:

For me, the edges are still too blurry for me to make out what this actually is. I need someone with more in-depth knowledge to let me know what is actually being proposed here.

On the optimistic side, this looks like a kind of "bigger step" in the direction that GPU/shader programming took, where you change the way you think about and break down a problem to get insanely fast results. Feels like if you target this interaction net structure and give it to this CPU that uses them natively, we could amplify the speed of computations to possibly allow for things that are currently way to slow to do. Realtime physics sims with magnitudes faster steps. That's pretty cool. And all of the downstream effects that would allow for, in product design, scientific modelling, etc. And that's just one train of thought.

On the pessimistic side, though, I have no clue how to "program for an interaction net". Seems like the authors took a "you don't need to, an LLM will do it for you" position, and I can get behind that, but that's a pretty huge step in the direction of "Natural Language Programming" in that I literally can't program it without using an LLM and natural language, because I don't understand the underlying details and probably won't have any structural support to understand it for a while, as the tooling slowly rolls out and gets iterated on, until it can do something we can recognize as "Debugging". I imagine there's some kind of "program it in C, and translate it" thing, too, but it feels like the point here is not to have me be able to debug it, and a detour through C just wastes LLM tokens.

So those are the initial impressions, but then I'm making a TON of assumptions in both sides of that. So I don't even know if my initial impressions are conceptualizing the right paradigms, much less if they are worth discussing with people who are seriously considering this topic. Only speaking for myself here, but at least my own silence is due to not having enough information myself, and not seeing enough in this paper to interest me in research in the topic just yet. Maybe if they've got something I can play with, I could get my head around it more. But, for now, it's just neat.

Top #2 — jkhdigital:

The title is a bit misleading—humans came up with all the insights and innovations here. What AI has done, which it is exceptionally good at, is take decades of brilliant ideas buried in research literature and synthesize them into a coherently engineered product. It would seem that AI is now doing an end-run around the innovator’s dilemma, or at least part of it, by dramatically lowering the R&D cost of productizing laboratory ideas.

Top #3 — pizza234:

I'm quite skeptical; their baseline is a in-order CPU, instead of a modern out-of-order design, and they're testing a small amount of programs.

Also, I'm not an expert in CPUs, but the underlying idea doesn't seem entirely novel - WaveScalar explored dataflow-based architecture 20+ years ago.

↳ reply 1 — kragen:

They're claiming better performance per watt, not better absolute performance, and out-of-order does worse on that metric than the superscalar in-order design they say they beat by 4.59×. That's why, for example, PULPino is in-order.

A third interesting metric is performance per transistor or per area, and generally the best designs there are the long-forgotten MISC designs like the MuP21 and the GA144.

↳↳ reply — adrian_b:

The performance per watt of very slow CPUs is always very good, so that alone is not impressive unless much more data is provided to prove that is really better than what is typical.

On the other hand, the performance per area of the "traditional" CPU that is used for comparison, which I assume that it is some kind of RISC-V, is very poor, so that the performance per area of the new CPU is likely to be also poor, even if much better than that of the strawman.

Their "traditional" CPU has an area that is slightly bigger than that of Cortex-A720 made with a CMOS process almost twice as dense.

So if they were made with the same process, the "traditional" CPU and the new CPU would have an area somewhat bigger than a half of a Cortex-A720.

But Cortex-A720 is an out-of-order 4-wide superscalar core with advanced SIMD and scalable vector extensions, with a good branch predictor and with many other enhancements, for which the area ratio in the same process is expected to be much greater than 2 in comparison with the CPUs evaluated in TFA, while its performance must be several times greater than that of a 2-wide in-order CPU core.

So both the "traditional" CPU and the Frostbite CPU appear to have a much bigger area than expected for their performance.

Moreover, the performance of in-order CPUs is very sensitive to the benchmark selection and to the quality of the compiler optimizations.

So the performance obtained for the benchmarks selected by them, like FFT or LU decomposition, is expected to be much better than for benchmarks that would execute an application not dominated by such regular loops, but having lots of hard to predict branches, e.g. a compiler benchmark.

They say that the ISA will be published. At that time it will be easier to appreciate whether this CPU architecture is really innovative. For now, they have done a lot of work, by fully implementing the CPU core, but the data presented is not sufficiently convincing to demonstrate that it is indeed an architecture that will be able to compete with SOTA CPU cores, e.g. with those from the Arm company.

↳↳↳ reply — kragen:

> The performance per watt of very slow CPUs is always very good

Generally this has not been my experience. Typically both very slow CPUs like the ATMega328 and high-performance CPUs like an Intel i7 are in the neighborhood of 1 nanojoule per instruction. (For operations more than 8 bits wide, the AVR is significantly worse.) Low-power CPUs like the STM32L line are commonly around 0.2nJ/insn. Ambiq's subthreshold logic gets them closer to 0.05nJ/insn.

I agree with the rest of your comment.

↳ reply 2 — rhdunn:

If you are interested in understanding how CPUs work there are a number of "build your own CPU" style video series on YouTube:

- Ben Eater's series "Building an 8-bit breadboard computer!": https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLowKtXNTBypGqImE405J2...

- Fabian Schuiki's series "Build a Superscalar CPU" (breadboard and custom boards): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLyR4neQXqQo5nPdEiMbaE...

- Polymath Unlimited's series "The CPU you can build (Tutorial Series)" (logisim): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLe8IZRJAn3oD3E2tDhNpI...

- mattbatwing's series "Let's Make a Redstone Computer!" (Minecraft): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5LiOvrbVo8nPTtdXAdSm...

item.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
item.description: 660 points, 308 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (kottke.org)

→ HN comments  ·  660 points  ·  308 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

Top #1 — seanhunter:

I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer.

There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand. I’ll give an example: compactness. Probably anyone who has done analysis is familiar with how this concept is usually taught. Typically how it goes is you do open and closed sets and then they hit you with “a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover”. Now this definition is extremely profound but very dense and it’s highly non-obvious why that in particular is the property you want (a finite subcover for every open cover)[1], how you could go about proving that every possible open cover in a certain situation could have a finite subcover etc etc.

In this case it’s actually quite easy to give simple explanations of the separate parts of the definition (open and closed sets, what an open cover therefore means, what a finite subcover then is etc) but actually understanding the concept of compactness requires something above and beyond whatever explanation you are given: it requires the reader to get out pencil and paper, try out some sets, go for some walks, think about it in the bath etc.

You may get a really fantastic explanation in simple terms from someone who deeply understands the topic, but if you don’t put in the effort you’re not going to understand it yourself. That’s not the fault of the explanation. It’s not an easy concept to grasp so you have to climb the ladder of understanding. The explainer can’t do that for you.

[1] it took the mathematical community years to settle on this being the definition, so you shouldn’t expect to understand why this is the definition straight away.

↳ reply 1 — stingraycharles:

I like to think that a “simple” explanation doesn’t necessarily have to be a short one. 3blue1brown is a good example of that. It took multiple videos for him to explain LLMs, but it’s simple and relatively easy to understand.

Actually, Feynman himself is a good example of that as well. His explanations are rarely short, but very simple. He has a series of YouTube videos where he explains all kinds of concepts like fire, but it still takes him at least 15 minutes to explain it.

So I’d argue that thinking it needs to be condensed into one or two sentences is getting the meaning of the expression wrong.

↳↳ reply — atoav:

A good explaination of a phenomenon is one where the people walk away from it and have the feeling of being able to grasp more of the nature of reality around them. You can make explainations short, but not too short.

An analogy I often like to use, is that an explaination is like a path up a mountain. You can have a long and winding, but comfy path, a direct stairway or a cliff without rope. The cliff may be the shortest, but it will select for the individuals that are used to climbing cliffs and even a fraction of those will struggle and fail on the ascent.

We educators are like mountain guides, people entrust us with selecting the correct route for them and we need to guide them up that route and make potential changes on the spot if we see a specific route doesn't work. If we do our job well, the people didn't even realize they were climbing a mountain, they were just entertained by us and the scenery. That is the goal. For this the path cannot be to short and not too long, it needs the correct length.

Of course that analogy is just that, but I like it. In real explainations order matters a lot. A good educator needs a real grasp on how concepts interconnect and rely on each other, so the order in which they are introduced make the path easier.

Bad educators just introduce concepts in arbitrary order or wrongly assume certain concepts to be "common knowledge" and thus a small hill at the foot of a mountain can quickly turn into a 9C+ difficulty climbing site.

↳ reply 2 — kccqzy:

Nah that is just not a good definition for beginners. It shouldn’t be somebody’s first introduction to compactness. There are other definitions that are less general but more intuitive, such as sequential compactness: every sequence has a subsequence that converges to a limit in the space. For beginners working only in metric spaces, there’s no difference anyways.

Directly teaching the most general definition misses the steps it took mathematicians to arrive at this definition and is unhelpful. In set theory classes nobody starts by teaching ZFC; instead we start by the general comprehension principle, discover paradoxes and then introduce ZFC.

That’s also the reason high schoolers taking an introduction to calculus class aren’t immediately taught the epsilon delta definition. Start with something more intuitive. Rigor can come later. Newton and Leibniz didn’t start with rigor either.

↳ reply 3 — Francute:

While I agree that the receiver needs to make an effort to understand, I don't think I agree with this explanation

Your definition; "a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover", requires a lot of prior knowledge to actually make sense of. When you say "explain it in simple terms", you are expected to explain all the needed concepts too

So what is a cover? what is an open cover? what is a subcover? what is a set!? heck, even what is finite/infinite? and what are all the new concepts you have to introduce to explain each of those?

The idea of explaining something in simple terms doesn't necessarily mean using a short, strictly formal explanation. It means making someone who is willing to pay attention understand everything (and this can usually be a long explanation). This requires a lot more effort than people usually think. Explaining forces you to remember concepts you assume others understands because with your own experience that feels already natural

In summary: - Don't confuse "compressing an idea" with "explaining it on simpler terms" - Explain it in a way an attentive 5 years old kid could understand

Top #2 — mr_mitm:

The article is just a bunch of quotes from Richard Feynman and John Gruber. There is little insight and I even think the article is misrepresenting the quotes.

Feynman said "if you can't explain it on a freshmen level". Leaving out that qualifier distorts the statement.

The other quote about the magnets is also overly reductive. Saying "I don't understand it in terms you're more familiar with" is not an admission that scientists as a group don't understand it at all.

You could go into what it means to understand something, but unfortunately the article isn't doing that.

↳ reply 1 — rocqua:

Besides, the claim on magnetic force already serves as a counter-example to the main claim of the article.

Unless the article means to say that Feynman didn't understand the magnetic force, they have to admit that the magnetic force was perfectly understood, but impossible to explain in simple terms.

↳↳ reply — programjames:

I think Feynman might have been referring to how spin was not understood (even by him), and magnetism is a result of a bunch of little spins adding up. I mean—even today—there are not really explanations that are correct and also understandable by a freshman. There's the belt analogy but, well, it doesn't really explain the physics.

↳↳↳ reply — mr_mitm:

That's not how I read it. Feynman started with the story of a girl going to the hospital because she broke something after slipping on ice. His point was that you can only explain things in terms that you simply accept without further explanation, otherwise you'd keep asking "why". Then he muses about imagining little rubber bands between magnets, but those only have their property in the end because of electromagnetism, so it's a circular explanation and thus unsatisfactory. To him, the magnetic field and its properties simply are, there is nothing underneath it.

↳ reply 2 — someothherguyy:

feynman talks about the idea in a more general sense several times in "surely you're joking mr. feynman"

Top #3 — tgv:

Explain to what level? E.g some topics common here. How do you explain NP in simple terms? "Things that are hard to compute?" That's simple, but not much of an explanation. It leaves the listener with a practically useless definition. And how do you explain even something practical as Heartbleed or Rowhammer? Etc.

And then there's another barrier, of course: the audience. You may use simple terms, and tell a lengthy story, but some things are hard to understand. Relativity and Monty Hall come to mind. They can be explained in simple terms, but how many people get them? Probably just the ones that also understand a detailed explanation.

↳ reply 1 — trash_cat:

Simple for your audience to understand. Which means you posses understanding deep enough that you can explain it any any level of detail.

↳ reply 2 — Dylan16807:

That's not a correct definition of NP. I would say you define P, and then say NP is where checking each answer/combination is P but you can try all of them simultaneously.

And I would say heartbleed and rowhammer are easier than that. There's only one or two steps to each problem.

Top #3 — lukeschlather:

The frustrating thing about this is now you can't take screenshots of a Signal chat on Windows. Yes, you can use screenshotting to get around retention or whatever, but that's a basic feature.

Another similar thing recently was I was trying to help a woman send a document to her lawyer, and for whatever reason I couldn't figure out how to share it with him via text or whatsapp. Somehow I was able to share it to my own phone via whatsapp, and from there I made a group text in Whatsapp with me and her lawyer to share the document.

With AI agents I think we're similarly getting into territory where it's not so clear-cut as Signal is making things out to be. I share the knee-jerk "keep your agents out of my stuff!" reaction but I don't think that's a sustainable/pragmatic choice. It might be correct as a principle but if it locks you out of the operating system, it's not Signal's job to disable key OS features on the grounds that the OS is insecure - at a certain point Signal might as well just wipe the hard drive, but that's not Signal's role. Signal is there to enable people to send messages, not stop them from doing so.

Top #1 — tito:

↳ reply 1 — smartmic:

↳↳ reply — andrewvc:

I wish we could afford to be very circumspect about geo engineering. There’s been too much warming to be slow about it.

↳↳↳ reply — chriswarbo:

The main problem with geoengineering is not the unintended consequences, the unknown unknowns, etc. It's that it would require massive, coordinated effort.

The reason I say that's the main problem, is because that's also the main problem with reducing fossil fuel usage.

It's fun to debate the technical details of geoengineering (solar shades, atmospheric aerosols, enhanced weathering, etc.), in the same way that it's fun to debate the technical details of carbon reduction (energy storage methods, approaches to electrical transmission, remote work, land use, etc.).

But none of that really matters if we, collectively, don't actually do anything! It's not as fun as comparing scifi fantasies, but the problem we need to solve is that of getting humanity to actually do something, at scale, which is collectively acknowledged as necessary yet is not immediately/individually profitable.

If we could solve that, then we could do geoengineering; but in such a world, we might not need to, because we could also do carbon reduction, plus a bunch of other stuff!

However, if we can't solve that, then geoengineering is an illusion.

It's a grass-is-greener fallacy: what makes any geoengineering project seem remotely feasible, in a world where we can't even coordinate on the obviously-a-good-idea stuff?
