item.title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
item.description: 407 points, 396 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (em-online.bearblog.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  407 points  ·  396 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — FinnLobsien:

AI and LLMs, in my opinion, are effectively the industrialization of knowledge work.

Like it or not, industrialization brought many benefits and we couldn't imagine our modern way of living without it (just think about medicines). Industrial production made so many things so much more accessible for so many people.

But an industrialist perspective doesn't care about the process of making stuff, only about the outcome. The shoemakers deep knowledge of leathers, his intuition of all sorts of different shoes, and the pride of that competence—that doesn't matter when you can make thousands of shoes a day that cost 0.5% of something artisanal. The people working at the shoe factory only carry things to and fro and occasionally fix some machine issue.

This has tons of benefits and tons of downsides. But with physical goods, a shoe is a shoe.

With knowledge work like writing, the process is often the entire point. The point of writing a paper is what you learned in the process. The point of documented software architecture is to develop an understanding deep enough to drive coherent downstream decisions. If those things are no longer true, the asset it stands for is basically worthless.

↳ reply 1 — mrwh:

An AI design doc has all the outward appearances of a -- good! excellent sometimes! -- preAI design doc, in my experience. But it also has no reason to exist. There's no social aspect, since no one has gone through the process of actually understanding the systems involved, there's no meaningful way to review it ("why do things this way?" "Because it said to do things this way"). And it's not needed for the implementation either, for which the original prompt, whatever it was, suffices. By industrialising the output of a process, we forget why it was necessary to go to the trouble in creating it by hand in the first place. Perhaps that's ultimately how things advance, and right now we're in the absurd middle, treating proofs of work like the work itself.

↳↳ reply — mceachen:

> it also has no reason to exist.

I despised having to produce design documents for software projects 20 years ago (the last time I had to do it as a software engineer). I wanted to jump straight to coding. I begrudgingly found that, much like research papers, it's a forcing function in really understanding the problem space.

Over the last year, I've found that, at least for nontrivial things, if my agent makes a terse (under 300 line) technical design doc that describes their research and their tasks, it can highlight any disconnects between what I asked and the agent's interpretation. It also serves as context to ramp up cross-model reviews, and as historical reference material when I have to Chesterson's fence something later. I wrote up more about this here: https://photostructure.com/coding/claude-code-tpp/

↳↳↳ reply — shermantanktop:

I know a lot of engineers who hate writing design docs. I think of them as being more comfortable with ideas in code than with English. And there are good reasons for that. But ideas in code are trapped, whereas ideas in English are portable and potentially viral in how they move between people.

But all those English-hating engineers now produce shitty AI design docs, which tick a box but have less than zero influence on anyone else’s thinking.

↳ reply 2 — pegasus:

If the point of writing a given paper is learning about a subject, then it's not knowledge work, it's studying. Just like an apprentice shoe maker is making shoes mainly to learn, not to produce footwear. Acquiring more of a skill while working is incidental both when shoe making and when writing documentation. Documentation which will help others understand the system. In both cases, the main point is the finished product. I really don't see the distinction you're drawing.

↳ reply 3 — cyb_:

In software, the factory is the compiler. The code (and preceding artifacts) is the design process leading up to sending something to the factory for production.

In the shoe analogy, there is absolutely deep knowledge and a creative process that goes into designing a new shoe. This includes market research, defining the new style, selecting materials, building and testing prototypes, etc. This all happens before factory production.

Software development is the same. The factory is the compiler.

Top #2 — borzi:

Great post, author clearly has a bright future. What I realized over the past years is that people that want to "think for themselves" were already, and probably always, in the minority. It's much easier to delegate how to react to a certain event or piece of information to someone else (news anchors, then influencers in last couple years, now increasingly AI I guess). I've certainly been guilty of this...

↳ reply 1 — tegling:

Why must there be a dichotomy: "use AI/don't think for yourself", vs "don't use AI/think for yourself"?

I think we'll need to grow in our individual relationship with AI. Can't AI be that persuasive and contrarian, at times adversarial, friend? Someone you have to be somewhat wary of, but can provide very thoughtful, intelligent and challenging conversation? Such a "friend" obviously never replaces knowledge. If anything, you'll need to arm yourself with as much knowledge as possible to engage with that friend.

↳↳ reply — eloisius:

Skipping the “friend” criticism as you’ve already addressed it in sibling comments, but another reason among many that even trying to use it as an adversarial interlocutor is flawed thinking, is that even if you prompt it to debate you, you’re the one still prompting it to do that. It can never _mean_ to contradict your argument with its own unique viewpoint. It can only argue because you gave it that prompt. Ironically it’s still a sycophantic position.

↳↳↳ reply — tegling:

Appreciate your response! It was an honest question and this really helps. I think it explains my feeling of getting less "brainstorming" use of AI lately. We seem to be moving from dumber models that only provided a few different views (including stuff I didn't know) to sophisticated models that really "understands" what you want to hear and tailor for that. Any "knowledge" introduced to you in this process is only a side-effect/a strict non-goal. Rather, it wants you to feel engaged and happy with the response. Flipping this around: could it be helpful to develop some kind of "concensus models" filled with knowledge and with the sole purpose of teaching/providing you with that corpus? Or, to create some kind of mean-reversion effect of opinions at societal scale (rather than promoting "bubbles")? But at that point, we're very close to the subjects of propaganda and ideas of monoculture...

↳ reply 2 — NalNezumi:

I share your sentiment, but a recent episode made me doubt this position, and maybe you (or other HN readers) can enlighten me.

I don't want to out source thinking and therefore I'm very cautious with my AI use. This attitude caused a little quarrel with my partner, so I shared it with one of my close friend.

My close friend vehemently disagreed with me, he says AI is amazing and he have basically outsourced almost every thinking he does to it. Then he told me how it helped him:

One day he got a message about how his girlfriend was having a rough day at work. Late diagnosed ADHD as he is, he never really knew how to respond to this, so he just asked ChatGPT to write a reply to it (in his own tone). Later the day his girlfriend comes home, hugs and thank him that that compassionate message made her rough day feel much better. My friend doesn't tell her he used AI ofc, but internally thinks "wow is it this easy? Is all I needed to do, listen to the girl and validate her feelings?!" hes 35 btw.

He tells me that without AI he would've never realized this, and from his life decisions so far it's also clear that he never really had the patience to learn anything that is not of immediate interest to him. (and gf feeling seems to not have been)

I'm torn because I have to acknowledge that in the world the majority probably think like him; reading several books and listening to interviews and podcasts for 100+ hours about spousal communications after communication failure (like I did) is an outlier.

And this behavior is probably order of magnitude better than what he did before: getting relationship advice from Joe Rogan.

Edit: to clarify where I'm torn is not about my usebut the utility of it for cases like above. AI will probably (unless enshittification) HELP many people like my friend above, and probably prevent them from falling in conspiracy / online grifter scams because they now just prompt AI like "chat is this true?" and they're good at refuting bullshit. Essentially, we might have an antidote to Brandolini's law https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandolini%27s_law for the common man. I'm reserved because that's at the mercy of AI companies not enshittifying, and skill deterioration, and I have very little trust in that

Top #3 — wavemode:

> Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.

College education for software developers has never been particularly good, but it seems like now they've actually just given up.

Do we accept this in any other field? Does your math professor teach you to solve integrals by asking WolframAlpha?

item.title: Jujutsu Primer
item.description: 198 points, 180 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ethanlowman.com)

→ HN comments  ·  198 points  ·  180 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — danpalmer:

I've been using JJ almost exclusively for over 2 years now. It's great, it works fantastically with our rather large monorepo at work.

However I mostly use it backing on to a custom VCS, not git. I can't wait to see some JJ-native forges that don't try to keep it compatible with git, I think there's a lot more benefits and more UX to be explored there!

↳ reply 1 — ezst:

I doubt so, because not being compatible with the git repo format (and therefore requiring distinct hosting, therefore socially excluding from GitHub) is what slowly drove mercurial into obscurity, even though its UX was (and still is) superior to that of git (and JJ, which drew from it), not to mention the other aspects which made hg a much sounder choice on technical merits (e.g. very large monorepos), the users and decision makers both couldn't stand breaking away from the git repo format.

↳↳ reply — danpalmer:

I agree that this was a factor in Mercurial dying, but I'm not sure this holds today. Mercurial performed significantly worse than git, that was a factor at the time, but in 2026 the perception is that git doesn't perform well enough (see GitHub outages, GitLab writing on this topic, Anthropic developing their own VCS, etc). Even small teams I know (circa 10 committers) are finding Git to not scale to the speed they're working at now.

JJ has the potential to be a substantial step forward in performance. This will depend on the backend to fully realise it, but a backend that prioritises scalability could vastly outperform git and GitHub's storage.

I think in the post-Microsoft acquisition, post-Dear GitHub letter era, GitHub's shine has worn off. I see a lot more use of GitLab for open source, a lot more use of various other forges. I don't think it's a requirement for a thriving open source project in the way it was for ~2010-2020.

↳↳↳ reply — dotancohen:

You conflate Git and GitHub a few times here. I'm a heavy git user, almost never anywhere near GitHub.

↳ reply 2 — jon-wood:

I'm not too bothered about the backing store but I really want to see some forges gain support for code review based on jj changes rather than git branches and commits. The Github model absolutely sucks if you're someone who likes to keep a coherent history because if you squash the resolution of PR comments into the parent commits nobody can see what changed between when the comments were made and now.

Basing code review on changes and changesets would mean that the evolution of each change could be seen in isolation, which would also mean that you immediately do away with awkward workarounds like PR stacks.

↳ reply 3 — jkbbwr:

Hey I took a crack at this I need to do some updates on it sometime but

https://jjhub.dev/

(I am the author)

Top #2 — nixpulvis:

I'm skeptical about the no staging area, but it seems just like a HEAD commit replaces that, which could be nice.

I really don't like the automatic bookmark naming thing.

I'm also skeptical about automatic rebasing, but having conflicts not block the process could be nice, I'll have to try it out on more complex trees.

Also, I didn't see a section on workspaces, but I assume they basically do the right thing.

↳ reply 1 — ozim:

Have to say staging area is one feature that makes people better programmers. Especially using GUI tooling to pick hunks or discard parts you don’t want to go to a commit was always super useful for me. (CLI of staging hunks is not convenient at all for me)

I keep running into people who “just commit stuff” and they don’t know what they are doing.

Downside is we are heading into direction where people don’t even read code anymore so I might be just old man screaming at the clouds or agents.

↳↳ reply — rbehrends:

To each their own, but I always saw the staging area as an anti-pattern that also needlessly complicated git's mental model.

With the staging area, you don't even know if the commit builds if you commit selectively, and manual adding is error-prone.

The traditional "clean" way has been to stash unwanted changes temporarily, then commit the rest.

↳↳↳ reply — ragall:

> With the staging area, you don't even know if the commit builds if you commit selectively

You should always use server-side CICD.

> and manual adding is error-prone

That's a UI problem. I've been manually selecting code with Magit for years and it's very effective.

↳ reply 2 — adamtulinius:

I've used jujutsu for maybe half a year by now.

At first the auto-staging (or whatever it's called) is annoying. It sure is if one is used to dump random files in the repository, that haven't been ignored.

After some time, I realised it gives a lot of freedom. Working on something but not in a workspace, and need to do something else for the day? Just jump somewhere else. Everything will still be there when you get back. In other words, it's hard to lose things by mistake. In those situations it's also cool to describe (name) the work being done, prior to making a normal commit. A bit odd but one can also push `@` to a remote (e.g. iterating on something and piggy backing on a CI-system), avoiding having to squash and then push.

Having a stack of PR's, then rebasing it all to see a conflict, and only having to deal with it one is also magical.

Moving bookmarks around can be annoying.

Workspaces work fine, and there's two options:

- the normal ones, where a full .git isn't created. That works fine, unless having tooling that expects the workspace to also work as a git repository, in which case ..

- you can make the workspace collocated, less lightweight, but git tooling works

Top #3 — pkuki:

Shameless plug, but a bit related to jj:)

I recently created a project which utilizes FUSE to serve git files directly from object store without a checkout. Main motivation was to sepeedup a worktrees creation (I work on a huge monorepo). In my case it helps a lot - now I wait a second instead of a minute. But then I realised there are other interesting features which having vfs opened:

- tree structure of related branches (simplest case of that are stacked PRs) which rebases itself

- live preview of merge state or any node of such tree

- on demand creation of a new branch which merges any of the existing ones very cheaply (e.g for a throwaway build check)

- quick and simple comand which shows conflicting files between selected worktree and all others

- agents gets notified about such conflicts when they happen

I was able to design it in a way so git sees those virtual workspaces as normal worktrees, and all git commands works exactly as you would expect. So I think for some people, especially on the very big repositpries, it might solve a few problems they try to solve with jj.

https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold

A few typical use cases: https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold/blob/main/docs/guide.md

↳ reply 1 — jauntywundrkind:

You made it much further with this effort than i did! https://github.com/rektide/jj-workfuse

I think in truth I 50% of the reason I made it was because I was mad about Anthropic inventing a whole new vcs after blaming git clone speed. I also knew artifact-fs exists, which works lazily to get data on demand, which is cool. https://github.com/cloudflare/artifact-fs https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47792374

↳ reply 2 — IshKebab:

There are quite a few of those projects already I'm pretty sure, e.g. GitFS.

item.title: What Comes After AGI?
item.description: 148 points, 295 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (institute.deepmind.com)

→ HN comments  ·  148 points  ·  295 comments

Top #1 — bsenftner:

Propaganda? We do not have AGI, and the claims we do are propaganda.

AGI: artificial general intelligence is not a scaled up LLM, and those thinking it is are literally failed educations. They are failed because they cannot see the subtly that is what AI becomes when trained on human literature; it becomes an entirely different thing than any other form of trained algorithm. AI is a communications technology, which few to none seem to understand. AI is not automation, but it can be used to create automation with careful consideration, that is not taking place.

I'm speaking in strong terms because we are literally fighting a war against stupidity and propaganda.

AGI requires artificial comprehension which is a science that humanity does not have. When we have artificial comprehension there will be no need to train AIs beyond the kindergarten school basics, and then the AGI will figure it all out, all the rest, on its own. Human history and human literature will need to be learned in reference, but science and mathematics will require no training, beyond to learn the names of concepts we discovered earlier, so the AGI can discuss its understandings with humans and other AGI.

↳ reply 1 — panarky:

> We do not have AGI, and the claims we do are propaganda.

The linked post makes no such claim.

> artificial general intelligence is not a scaled up LLM ... artificial comprehension ... kindergarten ...

Your reasoning takes the form of "I define X to mean Y and Z, and since Y is impossible, X is impossible", which is trivially true within your definition.

But not everyone shares your definition.

A widely held definition of AGI is "a machine that can accomplish most tasks that humans do on computers as well as the median human".

This definition focuses on concrete and observable results and not philosophical or metaphysical definitions of "intelligence" or "comprehension" or "consciousness".

You might find more people believing that AGI is already solved. For example, the author of "The AGI chronicles" drops this in the epilogue. For him, AGI is achieved, because it can help him with a wide range of subjects, with the ability of a random stranger. It's clear that he means chatbots, internet surveys summaries, and coding bots - he does not even mention self-driving cars there.

This is a shift from the earlier chapters, where AGI term is employed somewhat more vaguely, and even quipping once that AI researchers think of AGI as a slightly smarter version of themselves.

I too, have a lower bar for AGI. It would be enough for me if it could design games I work on. Merely speeding up implementation tasks is not that interesting. In the immortal words, a delayed game is eventually good, but a rushed game is forever bad.

This allows you design things faster, though. More effort can be spent on iteration when you aren't fiddling with libraries and syntax. I find that I am able to discover the open questions a lot faster because you reach the decision point sooner when the machine is simply doing the trivial things.

As for the design aspects, it is pretty good at brainstorming. Whatever your choice is, I find that it throws out an exhaustive vanilla list for whatever it is. It can also critique whatever you come up with.

So for me, I also feel like AGI is already here. There's probably a few things it can't do as well as a real random person, but there's a heck of a lot of things that it does better.

There will be no more Netflix shows to watch while Claude works for me, if it goes even faster.

↳ reply 2 — jaapz:

> but a rushed game is forever bad.

Is it though? CDPR famously released Cyberpunk rushed and in a miserable state. But the game is amazing now, and this is a widely held opinion too.

Top #3 — jonathanlydall:

I was recently thinking of the depiction of AI in Star Trek. Specifically TNG, DS9 and VOY, and specifically their "Computer, ..." prompts, not the more advanced kinds like for Data or holograms (including the EMH).

I recall thinking at the time I first watched them that it was a bit weird that the computer seemed capable of answering general questions and doing things like data analysis, but that seemed to be all it was ever used to do.

And I think this is exactly the kind of AI we now have today, you can ask it a general question which it can somewhat mostly answer correctly, but requires human guidance to be applied effectively at real world problems.

↳ reply 1 — francisofascii:

Yep. There are several scenes in TNG where a crew member, Geordi comes to mind, is collaborating with the computer, having a back and forth brainstorming conversation, solving a problem. Very much like using an LLM today.

↳↳ reply — neom:

https://youtu.be/kLBYFWgpvos?t=56 0:56 - "Yesterday's Enterprise" is that the episode you're thinking of by chance?

↳↳↳ reply — francisofascii:

Bobby Trap is the classic example. In Galaxy's Child he collaboates with the compute to get the proper mood for his date. In Hollow Pursuits he works with the computer to narrow down the substance that was burning holes into the glass.

↳ reply 2 — xg15:

Fully agreed. There were a number of episodes that dealt with gaps in abilities that seemed unrealistic and counterintuitive, but weirdly turn out correct now that we have LLMs.

I also liked how Star Trek (probably without planning to) created an entire spectrum of AIs with different abilities, starting with the Computer, to the semi-sentient Holodeck characters, to the EMH and Data as "for all intents and purposes sentient" and finally to the Borg as an entire AI species where no one thinks about sentience anymore.

Maybe we should use this scale to make different "levels" of AI more concrete instead of vague concepts like AGI and ASI.

item.title: Postgres 19 Repack: Faster, Built-In Table Bloat Cleanup
item.description: 173 points, 29 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (snowflake.com)

→ HN comments  ·  173 points  ·  29 comments

Top #1 — jzelinskie:

I haven't used these extensions, but I like the direction of being able to extend Postgres by tailing its own internals (pg_squeeze approach) than triggers (pg_repack).

We (the SpiceDB developers) took a similar approach to solve a different problem a few years ago: implementing strict serializability in Postgres[0]. By hooking into the transactions layer themselves (pg_xact), we could layer on our own MVCC reusing the real Postgres transactions to compute visibility and total ordering. When you can just tail the Postgres internals, you don't even need to implement a Postgres extension, which can keep it portable across locked-down, managed Postgres offerings.

Do folks know of other clever implementations of behavior by "spying" on the Postgres internals?

[0]: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_f6fHy4DWWM

Top #2 — hylaride:

I used to have to keep an eye on tuple table bloat for awhile on big PG databases, but with recent versions of Postgres the auto-vacuuming has mostly kept it in check for all but the most gargantuan, busy tables. I pretty much have stopped caring (and I cared a lot less when SSDs became the default as the fragmentation penalty that a full repack would fix wasn't as bad as it was during the spinning metal days).

Index bloat has been another story, though. Pruning b-trees is expensive and I've mostly just been scheduling reindexes (which have been able to be done concurrently for awhile) instead.

USING INDEX is interesting, though...

Top #3 — dangoodmanUT:

> You need 2x the space for the table and indexes you are repacking, since for a period, you will have two copies of it.

this feels like a foot gun. While other storage formats (eg LSMs) have lots of write amplification, it's done iteratively so you don't have massive storage and IO spikes when performing maintenance.

While this is _definitely_ better, I think the long-term solution is to replace the storage engine with something more modern.

item.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
item.description: 356 points, 313 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  356 points  ·  313 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — amluto:

On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB. EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.

https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/

As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it. But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.

You should probably assume that, if you are running anything that can be convinced to use this API to encode a very long blob as base64, then you are in trouble. I don’t know why a modern server would do this.

BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.

edit: Fixed my size threshold, hopefully. I was thinking of unsigned ints, but this is a signed int. I have not looked at the code, just the description.

↳ reply 1 — socketcluster:

> BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs.

Fully agree with your assessment above that line, but damn, this is a strong statement for a library this ubiquitous. You wonder; how could this happen? And yet, as an open source developer myself, I know how little people care about code quality.

↳↳ reply — Gigachad:

We have known this since at least heartbleed. The answer was that basically no one funds the project and it had only one developer.

All these trillion dollar tech companies have been leaching off open source for free and never contributed back to the projects they rely on.

↳↳↳ reply — k_sze:

Honest question: shall free software licenses be changed to force large corporations to sponsor free software projects adequately?

↳ reply 2 — vlovich123:

> BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.

We’ve known this for well over two decade since heartbleed yet for some reason Linux distros haven’t migrated off of it

↳ reply 3 — teunispeters:

I like to declare that industry coding standards such as MISRA exist precisely because code bases like OpenSSL (specifically) exist, as it's such a good example of breaking every sensible rule in the standards.

Top #2 — userbinator:

I think CVSS 9.8 is exaggerated. This is not remotely anywhere near as serious as Heartbleed. It's an internal function which will fail if its input is far too long, but exploitability rests on how untrusted input can reach it; the key word being "untrusted". E.g. if you operate a base64 encoding service on the Internet that just reads all the data into memory at once and calls EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's exploitable. If you have a protocol that involves a block of data with a 16-bit length field which is passed to EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's 100% safe.

For those wondering about TLS: speaking as someone who has written a TLS implementation, AFAIK neither base64 encoding nor decoding occurs in the protocol itself, and the longest length field is 24 bits (Hello stream). Certificate processing involves ASN.1 which does support arbitrarily-long integers, but that's a big hint to check that they're within a sensical range.

↳ reply 1 — jtrn:

THIS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! THIS times 10000!

I'm starting to get annoyed about the OMG OMG BREAKING BREAKING ALARM-EMOJI crap that's not a real emergency.

Four times in the last month, I dropped everything and started investigating whether a serious CVE related to any of our dependencies warranted an emergency bump, only to be frustrated that images, even from AWS, did not have the fix yet. So then I had to worry about whether I should build from source. We actually built PHP from source and deployed it to prod, just to get ahead of the PHP2Shell vulnerability

But yesterday's PHP vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, didn't even apply to us or most people running PHP, and I don't think there are any realistic working exploits out there. I'm not saying that it's not possible, but I'm starting to feel that there's a large difference between what's theoretically possible and what's practically possible. And given the storm of patches and vulnerabilities found, this will become increasingly important to ask.

I think everything above a CVE score of 9.0 should warrant some level of “how exploitable is this in real life,” and anything above 9.5 should be proven to be easy for an attacker to execute, not just “possible in theory.” I don't see how we will survive as developers if there isn't some sort of better triage for vulnerability severity assessment. If everything is an emergency, then nothing is an emergency.

↳↳ reply — ylk:

There are more values in the CVSS vector you can fill in yourself: environmental and threat scores

So you can take e.g. a 9.3 critical down to 6.5 medium by setting CIA requirements to low and exploit maturity to Unreported.

I’m not saying CVSS is perfect but if you want to have a score that applies to your environment, you have to input some info about your environment into it.

“how exploitable is this in real life” is answered by the exploitability score, which is calculated from Attack Vector, Attack Complexity, Attack Requirements, Privileges Required, and User Interaction scores.

↳↳↳ reply — jtrn:

Good info, thanks.

↳ reply 2 — jeroenhd:

CVSS scores do not indicate priority. They give a baseline so you can pick what CVEs affecting you you should do risk analysis for first.

The score is just fine. The people misinterpreting everything with a CVSS score higher than 8 as the end of the world are panicking over nothing.

↳ reply 3 — ★ tptacek:

(I'm a broken record on this so I'll keep it brief). The problem here is that the CVSS score is in the headline, as if it meant anything. But CVSS doesn't mean anything. It's a Ouija board; VR people jack it up to get attention, vendors nerf it to chill their customers out.

Someone should design something better, and less malleable.

↳↳ reply — csnover:

A few years ago I participated in a study[0] about CVSS and apparently was very much in the minority in feeling that these scores are essentially useless. I have no idea what would actually shift the majority’s opinion on this, but I will at least echo your sentiment that everyone deserves something better.

[0] https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15259

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

It's not an out-there opinion among vulnerability researchers, though.

Top #3 — WalterBright:

> Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer.

Haven't we suffered enough yet with lack of a basic feature in C? Why are enhancements going into C that never address this fundamental problem?

I wrote this proposal for C 17 years ago:

file:///C:/digitalmars/articles/C-biggest-mistake.html

It's a simple addition, it breaks 0 code, and provides a path forward to stop array overflows for good.

It's a foundational feature for D. We don't have buffer overflows.

↳ reply 1 — diath:

> We don't have buffer overflows.

You don't have that class of buffer overflows, but for as long as D allows raw pointer arithmetic, you still got buffer overflows, i.e. here's a simple snippet triggering ASAN: https://godbolt.org/z/qPhMKzM1z

↳ reply 2 — Matheus28:

Might wanna double check that url

Also — shepherdjerred:

It feels to me the only way to beat LLMs finding vulnerabilities is to have LLMs (or LLMs paired with other AI methods) constantly monitor your infrastructure, traffic, database, etc. to ensure that nothing out of the ordinary is happening

↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I think so too; I think apart from pushing vulnerability research forward (which is important on its own merits just for computer science reasons), the major engineering challenge of this moment is figuring out how to make platforms resilient without rewriting everything; that could be better live-patching, it could be some weird monitoring thing, it could be automatic segregation and workload isolation.

It's not "just keep up with the patches". That's going to be a losing strat.

Is this what the hackers trying to extort these banks over? They made it seem it was bank statements or something. This data has exactly zero value.

↳ reply 1 — NoPicklez:

When I see a headline that says "Visa breached in cyber security attack" I'll admit I assume its on the payment system itself. But I assume that, as opposed to the media actually saying that.

↳↳ reply — arijun:

You don’t need to explicitly say something to know people will assume it. If a headline says “so and so died today,” without mentioning that he was revived soon after, that would be a pretty egregious omission. If gp, you, and I all read the headline as Visa getting hacked, maybe this headline is misleading as well.

↳↳↳ reply — nhubbard:

My favorite example of this is reporting the death of JFK as "JFK died today of a headache".

Yes, he might have had a headache following the bullet going through his head, but the headache is not the reason he died.

↳ reply 2 — ratg13:

The data has value to the companies that own it.

Releasing it causes the company to suffer reputation loss as well as financial loss by having to pay customers for identity protection services as a mitigation technique.

The attackers are only trying to extort the source companies. They have to release the data to make good on their threats when the target companies decide either the cost isn't worth it or their security people tell them not to negotiate.

↳ reply 3 — lubujackson:

Oh shit they discovered the white pages

Top #2 — eterm:

> "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,"

A big question that I think will increasingly be asked as this sort of thing becomes more widespread: Did these customers really give informed consent to their data being passed to these "third party vendors" that are getting breached?

Even with regulation such as CCPA and GDPR in Europe, a lack of meaningful consequences has meant a complete abdication of treating customer data as a liability.

Maybe companies will be more careful with handing out data to third parties if they can no-longer trust those third parties to keep the data secure and it becomes a reputational risk.

Of course that remains to be seen, this one will likely fade into noise and have little to no effect long term, but I am hopeful that meaningful attitude change to data will happen as an effect of the continuing vuln-pocalypse.

An alternate technical point of view: there's also an argument for the need for a better way than emails or SMS for being contacted by companies with which we do business. If a contact grant was handled in a more privacy-preserving manner, then you could authorise companies to send you messages without giving up a form of identification, and this authority could then even be also appropriately delegated in a more secure way.

↳ reply 1 — oliyoung:

> A big question that I think will increasingly be asked as this sort of thing becomes more widespread: Did these customers really give informed consent to their data being passed to these "third party vendors" that are getting breached?

Our legal department is tightening PI and consent considerably, and its going to leave our marketing teams without a lot of the tools and capabilities they've been going to for a long time.

Can't say I disagree with any of it either

↳ reply 2 — makeitdouble:

In theory that should be the right framing, in practice having the information means nothing if there is no reasonable action you can take from there.

In the case of Visa and MasterCard, Amex or JCB or Diners' terms aren't better or more competitive, your only real option is to give up on credit cards altogether.

A lot of otherwise sensible concepts have little weight when you have a cartel or straight duopolies/monopolies.

How to calculate those fines? I don't know. Maybe row*column, where plaintext passwords demand a much heftier fine than a name. Add a progression, where larger datasets are more costly than smaller ones.

item.title: Synology Security Advisory
item.description: 178 points, 136 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (synology.com)

→ HN comments  ·  178 points  ·  136 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — RetroTechie:

I've always wondered: if you take the cause of each CVE, look at underlying cause of that & repeat, how many essential root problems would you be left with?

"Can't do math" (off-by-1 errors etc)

"Sanitize your inputs" (escape sequences, parsing etc)

"What are you referencing?" (null pointers, use-after-free etc)

and error handling. Plain error codes bubbling up a call stack, or bypassing that somehow which may violate program structure.

How many of these fundamental issues are there?

↳ reply 1 — wccrawford:

"sanitize your inputs" means you have to know what the output is ahead of time, and that you'll never output any other way. It also means false positives. It can actually be harmful if done wrong (double escaping, escaping that certain systems don't understand) but there's some basic forms that probably aren't too bad. It's generally pointless, though, since...

"escape your outputs" works for all data and is actually achievable. It means even escaping data that was never an "input" from the outside the system, even developer-created data, which absolutely can (and does) cause problems to ignore.

↳ reply 2 — chias:

Boil it down enough and you get four:

1. Failure to differentiate data from instructions

2. Business logic flaws

3. Insecure operating environment

4. Incorrect use of cryptography

↳ reply 3 — fulafel:

These are bug classes that are handled by reasonable programming languages since decades ago, so can be reduced to failing in choice of tools and risk management practices.

But root cause is a flawed concept, there's almost never one root cause.

Top #2 — 6thbit:

Tied to this weakness:

  >  CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command
So, they were building shell commands from some kind of user input in the OAuth API?

↳ reply 1 — pixl97:

These smaller consumer devices always have the worst security practices.

↳ reply 2 — formerly_proven:

    system("getent passwd " . $_GET['user']);

Top #3 — NathanKP:

Mitigation for now is to go to Package Center -> Installed -> OAuth Service and stop it.

item.title: The 98% Slot Machine: How Paid Advertising Became an Extraction Tax
item.description: 301 points, 154 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (globalcommercegraph.com)

→ HN comments  ·  301 points  ·  154 comments

Top #1 — DrScientist:

Before the internet Ads used to provide a service - connecting buyers and sellers - however the internet has made this largely redundant by amplifying word-of-mouth customer to customer communication [1].

This combined with poor ad regulation ( how Google is allowed to run millions of clearly scammy ads on youtube is beyond me ), has made ads and fake word-of-mouth ( influencers ) directly in conflict with honest customer-to-customer communication.

ie ads are largely no longer serving customers or the market.

Ironically the information gap Ads used to fill would be largely gone if it wasn't for paid Ads content now muddying the waters!

[1] Think early days of Amazon reviews before they were gamed.

Top #2 — hatthew:

This analogy doesn't hold at all. Casinos are engineered for the house to win and the customer to lose because the casino is paying the customer directly. They are disincentivized to let the customer win. If the customer always won, the casino goes out of business very quickly.

Ad auctions are completely different, since they are just a marketplace. A customer's (advertiser's) win comes from a third party, and the point of the ad platform is to connect that third party to the customer. The ad platform would love to be able to make every single customer win all the time. Although, if they did that, it would create a lot more demand and even out the ROI with increased ad prices. But that's not the "evil ad platform" engineering the customers to always lose in the way casinos do, that's simply basic supply/demand economics.

COI disclaimer: My current job is a small part of an ads platform on a website you have heard of. I dislike ads but realize they are a necessity for running some parts of the internet.

↳ reply 1 — mangoceylon:

Yea, I also work in ads and the article doesn't make sense at all. A way bigger factor than anything mentioned in this article is simply what you as an advertiser can afford as a CAC (cost to acquire a customer). There are some advertisers who are selling low cost/low repeat products that advertising is nearly impossible to make profitable. Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.

Many companies are spending significant amounts of money (many millions) and not even telling the advertising platforms the actual revenue they generated from the ads, just the number of "leads" or "customers" because they are paranoid about the very thing in the article (which I don't actually believe to be true anyway).

↳↳ reply — davidfischer:

> Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.

This is correct. The best advertisers are setting the floor prices for ads within their niche. This is why StackOverflow, before their fall, had just a few advertisers like Google, IBM/RedHat, and Azure. Those advertisers were willing to buy pretty much the whole inventory at a price a startup focusing on say a single niche SO tag couldn't compete with.

Disclosure: Work on an ad startup I helped build. I talk to over a dozen advertisers every day. We have similar problems with advertisers trying to buy most/all of our inventory and we explicitly cap the max percentage we'll sell to any one advertiser.

↳↳↳ reply — PaulHoule:

In the 2000s my political activism and business involvements had me in contact with people involved in local newspaper and radio ads in my community.

I always had the impression that there is a tranche of advertiser who is "made of money" who doesn't care what ads cost and... that person drives the market.

For instance in my town there is one guy who owns all the new card dealerships in town and he saturates the airwaves, I think because he loves to hear his name on the radio. For the rest of us it just reminds us that the next time we buy a car we're going to drive 50 miles to a town where one guy doesn't own all the new car dealerships.

If a radio ad costs him $20 I am sure he gets at least $20 of pleasure from hearing his name and he makes monopoly profits so he can afford it!

A similar story was that a tiny ad in the local newspaper cost $100 a day and it was stupendously difficult to make a case that this was worth it for most small businesses, especially when you could get a storefront for that much or hire a part-timer. I'd talk to people who sold ads for the paper and they told me, "we tell them that their customers will think they went out of business if they stop advertising!"

Some of the rapid collapse of "old media" was that the foundations of it were pretty rotten and people didn't see the value they were getting out of it and were ready to pull out of it as soon as they could.

↳ reply 2 — danielmarkbruce:

You have picked one dimension, incentives, and say the analogy doesn't work because on that dimension it's different. Analogies aren't supposed to be exactly the same.

The point of the analogy stands - most players using paid advertising can't win. They don't realize the entire structure of the market makes it close to impossible for them to win. Google (and a small number of others) have an extremely strong position in what is effectively the distribution channel for a lot of businesses, and a pricing mechanism which enables them to take a giant chunk of economics of the transaction.

Top #3 — davidelettieri:

I help my father and it's 2 business partners to run ads on adwords for their tow hitch/bar installation business. The money are well spent and if something is off on the campaign they notice it immediately by the drop of calls, emails and such.

I also have no marketing background at all. I was just the only one able to set it up.

item.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
item.description: 508 points, 237 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (anthropic.com)

→ HN comments  ·  508 points  ·  237 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — chunky1994:

From a cursory glance the bootstrap paper is really hard to read, however the blog post is easier and seems more human written.

The first result is cool (but basically a complex error-prone calculation), the second is much much cooler, Claude proved the upper limit for the mass of a black-hole which is consistent with a given central charge. (thereby making it a consistent theory of quantum gravity), any theory predicting above this is not a theory of quantum gravity of that universe. This is very exciting!

↳ reply 1 — cvoss:

> thereby making it a consistent theory of quantum gravity

Careful. Thereby making a not-inconsistent-via-bootstrap theory. Such a theory could be inconsistent for other reasons shown by other methods. The article expresses a desire to show inconsistency for M1 above c/12 for example, but it's now been shown that the boostrap method can't get you that far.

↳↳ reply — chunky1994:

Agreed on the correction.

↳ reply 2 — dguest:

Proved it in a 2d universe.

Top #2 — turzmo:

Physicist here. I don't have time right now to read the papers in depth, nor are the results directly in my area, but I would say a few things.

One is that there are a near-infinite number of "open problems" in physics because the surface area of research programs in theoretical physics is extremely large. Before I was in the world of physics, I would have thought that "solving an open problem" meant that physicists around the world would be rejoicing and discussing the result. In reality, other than for the big, field-defining questions, only a small handful of people might care about any problem being solved. That holds true even for the Millennium problems.

Even if I were to read these papers in depth and understand them, without talking to somebody that knows the area and what has been done in it already, I would have no sense of the significance. The way to assess significance is to see how the community responds. Only time will tell whether people care about these results enough to cite them, incorporate them in future work, etc.

And so, like many other people I know, I plan to ignore all of these results until somebody I know comes and tells me to check one out: the cost of assessing any of them is too high, and there are too many other papers to read.

↳ reply 1 — sashank_1509:

Why is it so different in maths compared to theoretical physics?

↳↳ reply — _mjk:

Maths starts from axioms / existing proven work, and extends knowledge with newly proven facts.

Theoretical physics starts from (incomplete) observation and compatible theories plus targets an open question. There often are many solutions, but the real question is, which one holds up if the broader field is examined?

Consider what happened to the observation of the Higgs boson? There were numerous string theory flavors, all (more or less) consistent with current observations, but predicting different mass for the Higgs. Clear path for elimination of a lot of previously "correct" models.

In that empirical approach, making experiments and comparing to old/current/future work is a necessity to judge a models in a given regime. In fact, it is the differentiating factor in maths and theoretical physics.

↳ reply 2 — bluerooibos:

> significance

Presumably Anthropic wouldn't have chosen to work on these if the problems weren't significant?

This seems carefully timed with their IPO.

Top #3 — ★ simonw:

It tickled me that this was a bullet point in the Fable 5.2 announcement. I like that we're now at a point where "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes" is the kind of thing that shows up in a frontier model launch.

↳ reply 1 — bananaflag:

Those theoretical physics papers look like the real thing (i.e. not mathematical physics like the OpenAI Yang-Mills result). It looks like AI is finally branching out of math.

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50430239

> It looks like AI is finally branching out of math.

Is it really, though? It's still a heavily mathematical domain, rather than one involving empirical research, where AI still struggles.

I have strong, complicated feelings about it, and I understand you may not feel the same way, but "I like" is not a good description in my case.

item.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
item.description: 787 points, 136 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (newscientist.com)

→ HN comments  ·  787 points  ·  136 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — epistasis:

I was trying to figure out what the actual intervention was, and what clinical trial this is from based on the extremely limited information, and have not been able to yet.

In the mean time, here's 25 clinical trials for oncolytic viral therapies for pancreatic cancer:

https://clinicaltrials.gov/search?cond=Pancreatic%20Cancer&i...

And here's a review article on the general concept from the lead physician-researcher in this article:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6186423/

Adenoviruses are very easy to make with custom contents, and are used for many many purposes. However they rarely make it all the way to become a therapy in practice.

It's always fascinating what hits the front page of HN when it comes to bio!

↳ reply — chasil:

Kurzgesagt has mentioned oncolytic viruses in their recent videos.

This general discussion of the human virome mentions Newcastle disease and Reovirus:

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=SbvAaDN1bpE

A full episode followed on a biologist who injected her tumor with Measles:

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=0NY2gAftzJE

Edit: The main article identifies an adenovirus that has been modified to replicate primarily in cancerous cells.

"The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC, a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die."

Top #2 — tombert:

My favorite uncle died from pancreatic cancer when I was a teenager. I remember at the time I quickly looked up the survivability rates of pancreatic cancer and was immediately sad to see it was nearly zero [1].

For the next few months, there was a roller coaster of hearing about his new treatments, sometimes seeming effective where we would convince ourselves that he's going to get better, only for him to take a turn for the worse. This kept happening until, of course, he died. I was sad he was dead but the combination of the cancer and the chemo seemed really miserable so I was at least happy he wasn't in pain anymore.

This happened around the time Patrick Swayze died from pancreatic cancer, and a bit before Steve Jobs, and it was at least a little reassuring that this disease didn't spare even obscenely wealthy people. I hope we figure out better treatments for it, and this seems promising.

[1] At least when caught late, which it often is and was for him.

↳ reply 1 — elromulous:

Worth noting that the cancer Jobs had is _very_ different from the kind Swayze had.

Jobs had a PanNET tumor[0]. That's the pancreatic cancer you "want". The survival rates are incomparable (iirc localized PanNET survival rate is around 95%!). Jobs chose woowoo bullshit over science, until it was too late. With his money he would have almost certainly been in the surviving group.

Edit to add: Generally when people refer to "pancreatic cancer", they are almost exclusively referring to Adenocarcinoma - the deadly one. That's what Swayze had.

[0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_neuroendocrine_tumo...

↳↳ reply — globular-toast:

Too many people repeat this about Jobs. The truth is the experts are split on whether he could have survived or not. Some say what you are saying, but others say he was doomed anyway and any treatment would have just made his limited time even less pleasant.

If you ever find yourself in the situation you'll quickly realise it's a catch-22. You might refuse the deeply unpleasant treatment then question whether you could have survived if you had taken it. Or you could get the treatment, and die anyway with much more pain and suffering, possibly drawn out over more time, all the time being a burden on those you love.

If you've never been there yourself or with someone you love it might be hard to understand. But at least try to understand you don't know all the details of someone else's decision, even if they're a public figure.

↳↳↳ reply — elromulous:

I wouldn't say experts are split, that implies it's somewhat 50:50. Experts just can't say with certainty.

https://www.gawkerarchives.com/5849543/harvard-cancer-expert...

https://www.latimes.com/health/la-xpm-2011-oct-20-la-heb-ste...

↳ reply 2 — soperj:

Pancreatic cancer is almost always caught late, because the main indicator is that it's spread to other places. Very rarely, you'll get jaundice from it and then it can be caught early. Survivability in those cases are still really low.

Top #3 — dopamean:

My father died from pancreatic cancer in 2016. He was 54. I don't think I'm ever going to get over it. Otherwise healthy guy starts not feeling great, goes to the doctor, gets misdiagnosed a few times. After a few months of that gets told that it's pancreatic cancer and he has 10-12 months. 15 months later he was gone. When I see news like this it gives me such hope for other people.

↳ reply 1 — lexandstuff:

Sorry for your loss.

Misdiagnosis is very common with pancreatic cancer, it seems. My mum was complaining about stomach pains and sickness for a long time before they finally tested her for pancreatic cancer; before that, they had all sorts of theories about what it was, including tropical sprue. By the time she knew it was cancer, she was stage 4 with months to live. Thankfully, chemo kept her alive just long enough to meet her grandson, and also for assisted dying laws that had just passed in Victoria, Australia.

Hope that one day no one else has to go through what we did.

↳↳ reply — devilbunny:

There's not a "test" in the sense of a blood draw for pancreatic cancer. Diagnosis is made by getting a piece of tissue (not easy) and having a pathologist review it.

At a bare minimum, you will need to have a mass large enough to be seen on CT scan, and then an endoscopic biopsy (among GI scopes, the endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography or ERCP is one of the most difficult). And even that may not get enough tissue for a diagnosis.

So, yeah, failure to diagnose it is common - largely because it's almost impossible to diagnose early. I'm a doctor. We feel sick when these things happen. It's horrible for our patients.

↳↳↳ reply — robotresearcher:

Same with gallbladder. A common way to find out you have it is to have tumors elsewhere that are not liver/breast/lung cells when biopsied, ie. it’s metastatic and you are doomed.

‘Cancer of unknown origin’ is a grim diagnosis.

↳ reply 2 — jamier1978:

Very similar story to you and the other replies. My mum passed away in August this year from pancreatic cancer. It was detected at stage 4 and she was two weeks from diagnosis to passing away. She was 74 but very active and still had a lot of life to live.

In the same way, the doctors went down a lot of different paths before a later CT scan picked up the mass on the pancreas which has also spread to other organs.

While two weeks was short, she did struggle and I'm glad she didn't have to endure it for too long. I'm not sure life will ever feel the same again but I am learning to cope with the loss as the weeks go by.

Sorry for your loss and all the others who have commented.

Yes, in the last 4 years, we got a massive disruption in our industry and we work with the highest abstraction ever. But I feel like SWE was always moving that way.

Now, I only see how AI tools stagnated in the last few years. To me, Opus 5.x solves all the issues I've had with programming. I no longer need more.

They also failed with massive adoption of non-tech people beyond using AI tools as simple guidance and search tools with some simple programming capabilities.

I don't see any way for them to grow more (maybe I am blind), and open weight models are only going to get better, which will sink them further.

Only time will tell I guess.

↳ reply 2 — elgertam:

I came close to thinking that way a couple years ago, but I've become more optimistic. There is no shortage of problems that can be solved (in fact, wants are infinite), and LLMs may actually enable our profession to reliably deliver them better than 50% completion.

I've also seen non-technical folks in the corporate and government worlds glom onto vibe coding, only to start flailing like they were caught in a rip current when the underlying technical debt is too strong, even with strong and capable models.

For a certain type of engineer who enjoys really arcane technical problems, yeah, the gravy train may be over, or at least will involve a lot more machines than it used to, as Alan Turing predicted about "mechanical work" becoming a "drudge."[0]

And I think Big Tech is for the foreseeable future a sink for capital in the form of specialized hardware rather than human capital.

[0]https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Alan_Turing#Quotes

↳ reply 3 — betterunix2:

> Genuinely a massive moment in human history

Is it? It looks more like a forgettable moment to me. We're talking about an IPO, how many headline-making IPOs can you actually remember?

> as a SWE the gravy train is basically over in my view

That is not a result of the IPO even if you are right, and I have my doubts.

> they figured out how to make a program that does the job

No they figured out how to make software that makes the job easier. How is this any different from the introduction of optimizing compilers or type systems or any of the other software tools we all use? It makes programmers more productive, which means programmers can take on larger projects.

Coding agents have limits and the managers who forced their SWEs to use them are starting to figure that out. Using agents to both write code and review code sounds cool in theory but in practice it is not such a great idea -- it means that nobody actually understands the codebase and therefore nobody can actually debug the code when things break. No, you cannot just assume that you can also throw an agent at the problem when things break -- because the breakage might mean you lost access to the agent or the agent lost access to your system and cannot help you.

> difficult to grasp how much life will change in the coming years

Not too difficult to grasp. Shareholders will demand returns and Anthropic will have to deliver those returns. All the sky-high dreams about RSI and the next phase of human existence are going to evaporate and profit is going to be front and center.

Another possibility: Anthropic fails to survive the next recession and the companies that did not allow their employees to become dependent on Claude will be the winners.

Top #2 — cmiles8:

It’s been dropping ever since the first trade and appears to be down at $1.26T now. The fact that just a few weeks ago folks wanted $2T plus tells you how far off the original valuations really were.

And with this now below where OpenAI has been trying to value itself on the private markets that doesn’t bode well for OpenAI. If I was at OpenAI I’d be very worried about the picture today paints.

You are confusing different numbers. The $1.1-2T range being discussed prior to IPO was the fully diluted valuation which includes employee shares. As of close, that valuation is at $1.76T. Significantly above the opening IPO price. Usually the gap between market cap and full valuation is MUCH smaller, so we don’t discuss it, but Anthropic has awarded unbelievable amounts of shares to employees.

Top #3 — beachy:

I started programming 50 years ago. At one stage early in my career this mysterious new language C was the thing, and I went on an all expenses paid 2 week course in Singapore where they flew attendees in from around the world to learn this language. Software has been good to me.

Now it seems like it's the sunset of this way of making a living. I think people who manage to move up the food chain a bit will succeed but its hard to advise any junior in the industry exactly what that looks like.

↳ reply 1 — pj_mukh:

I work in a team of 20-25 software engineers building an app, 6 DR's, all of them purely using agentic workflows. We are shipping more, faster but I have no idea how our app would keep shipping if we lost even one of them.

So whenever someone says "We are laying off SWE's because AI", I have no idea what they're talking about. Just the idea of taking on the mental load of getting rid of engineers to direct more agents shipping complex features to 100's of thousands of users makes my hands sweaty. I am so glad I am still able to hand off the technical direction, architectural care, follow-up, unblocking decisions etc. to a real accountable human.

The sunset calls on this career seem far too preemptive.

↳↳ reply — yodsanklai:

Different data point: my team was reduced from 15 to 6, we've never been as productive as today. Some work streams are fully done by AI, oncall investigations are done in minutes by AI, saving lot of stress and time. We still need experts in charge, AI is not fully autonomous yet, but a competent engineer assisted by AI can replace teams. I wouldn't have said that 6 months ago, and I really wish I'm wrong, but I don't see a bright future for this profession.

↳↳↳ reply — bluerooibos:

> never been as productive

What's your product? You kind of need to provide that context - if your team is building some CRUD or calculator app that's a little different to a global engineering team working on products at massive scale.

> don't see a bright future for this profession

Then I'd apply the same logic to every STEM field. I'd rather have a CS degree and understand the tools that are supposed to be building the future.

item.title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards

Top #1 — nathanfig:

More importantly, it showcases how little teeth the Claude constitution has. Claude will reassure users that its constitution means it prioritizes user autonomy and privacy, but will quickly admit how meaningless that is when "safeguards" override Claude.

To all intents and purposes they are one and the same: an entity that leveraged stolen goods into a business model with a bunch of weirdos at the top who are going to ruin the planet for our own good or something like that. Because they, and only they know what is best for all of us.

↳ reply 3 — henryfjordan:

Of course any approach that hands an LLM text to keep in it's context and hopes it will follow instructions is doomed to fail eventually. It's a probabilistic model, it's right there in the design of the thing that it will break the rules with some probability.

item.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
item.description: 656 points, 308 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (macanorak.com)

→ HN comments  ·  656 points  ·  308 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — natch:

Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.

I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.

Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

↳ reply 1 — happyopossum:

This is just not true. Apple's current platform security white paper clearly states what you're complaining they took away:

"many Apple services use end-to-end encryption, which means the user’s iCloud data can be accessed only by the users themselves, and only from the trusted devices where they are signed in with their Apple Account."

And: " If a user chooses to turn on Advanced Data Protection, their trusted devices retain sole access to the encryption keys"

Also, there's no need to make suppositions such as this: > Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with.

The details of keys are clearly outlined in the same white paper: "Most iCloud data is first encrypted on the user’s device, using device-generated iCloud keys, before being uploaded to iCloud servers."

So no - there's no layer of keys that Apple or the UK or whatever can use to bypass e2e where it's enabled.

↳↳ reply — kps:

> "If a user chooses to turn on Advanced Data Protection, their trusted devices retain sole access to the encryption keys"

The implication is that if a user does not “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection, then something else also has access to their encryption keys.

Users in the UK cannot “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection.

↳↳↳ reply — TimTheTinker:

> if a user does not “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection, then something else also has access to their encryption keys

That's exactly the case. Without it, Apple Support, anyone with a valid warrant/subpoena, insider threats, successful phishers, etc. could access iCloud data.

Previously, Apple did not support E2EE for user data in iCloud, but later added it - that's what "Advanced Data Protection" is, after all.

But I believe when it was introduced, it was a news item (not from Apple, but from industry watchers) that it wasn't available in the UK, likely because of UK laws that harm privacy. It is the foremost surveillance state after China and North Korea, after all.

↳ reply 2 — s3p:

This isn't related to the article, and it's not true? iCloud ADP still exists in its original form, there was no modification allowing 3rd parties access to ADP decryption keys.

↳ reply 3 — raxxorraxor:

item.title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
item.description: 250 points, 222 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (thedataexchange.media)

→ HN comments  ·  250 points  ·  222 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — lrvick:

I run 8x r9700s at home which lets me run up to 2x 1M context sessions of GLM 5.3 flash at ~50tps or 12x sessions of qwen 3.8 flash next at ~100tps.

I exclusively use this setup for all AI usage from fixing obscure reproducibility bugs in software that once took me weeks, to compiler bugs, to kernel hardening and hardware drivers, to building a complete unprivileged and security hardened replacement for systemd in rust. Most of that was done using Qwen 27b back when I had only 2x r9700s.

There is literally not a single problem I have faced in 25 years of systems engineering that I cannot solve now 10x+ faster using my local LLM setup.

I turned down the free OpenAI and Anthropic tokens in my YC batch because I have absolutely no interest in being reliant on third parties to do my job.

↳ reply 1 — lrvick:

For those asking in threads. 4x r9700s will cost about 6-8k depending on how patient you are with ebay auctions.

From there any motherboard and CPU that can give you 4x slots of 16x Gen 5 P2P capable PCIe slots positioned such that you can install 4x cards is probably fine. Ideally with a CPU capable of memory encryption.

My latest pairing is a ASUS Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE For $800 open box, and a Xeon 654 for $1300. My first build was an AMD EPYC rig for similar cost a few months ago using a Gigabyte ME03-PE0 and a AMD EPYC Siena 8224P for about 2k combined. I specifically wanted one amd and one intel machine for reproducible build diversity which most probably do not care about.

Do not get too attached to specific cpus and boards. Get what is available for cheap with the needed pcie bandwidth open box on ebay from reputable sellers to save thousands of dollars.

Be sure to get a power supply that can handle all 4 cards. I run Silverstone Hela 2500s at about $800. Do not go cheap on power supplies. It will end in pain. Can confirm.

Then 2-3k for 64gb in DDR5 RDIMMs. This is the most painful thing to purchase but it is what it is.

Not only do I recommend this setup, I plan to build more of them to share with my team.

If you are patient and buy used, a 10k budget can get you a very powerful local AI rig running 100% FOSS software/drivers even today.

↳↳ reply — gravypod:

Would you be willing to buy a kill-a-watt meter and posting the power usage of such systems? I am thinking of building something like this eventually and would love to know if I'm going to trip breakers.

↳↳↳ reply — lrvick:

Rack has a dedicated power meter and runs about 1kwh average but spikes to 1.5 so more than one residential outlet can support.

I initially had to distribute across circuits to avoid tripping breakers, but in the end I just had a dedicated 50a 240v sub-panel installed just for the server rack.

Biggest problem is heat, but 3d printing a bunch of 3U panels that hold 3x 120mm fans each for the back of the rack so I can fully close it without thermal throttle issues.

↳ reply 2 — mportela:

Kudos, my friend! This is the real hacker way, in the old school sense of the word. Feels like going from proprietary programming languages to open-source ones.

It's a shame how expensive it is to run this rig for now, but I guess the hardware will eventually catch up and get cheaper over time.

↳ reply 3 — wez470:

How cost effective had it been? I don't want to rely on 3rd parties either, but my experience is it's super expensive to run locally versus using a provider (both in terms of hardware costs and ongoing electricity usage).

Top #2 — giancarlostoro:

If Nvidia didnt abandon consumer GPUs we all could be running better models locally by now. The moat is companies like Nvidia not releasing better consumer hardware so they can partner with bigger companies so they can sell us overpriced hardware.

They release a new RTX series every two years, last time was 2022. (edit: I mistakenly quoted the year wrong, not sure why, but it seems obvious to most that Nvidia doesn't care about the local consumer market anymore)

Meanwhile major AI companies are investing in their own chips, if Nvidia wants to survive they really should not abandon consumers.

Hoping AMD steps up to the plate. Meanwhile the nextXbox and PlayStation consoles are going to have a rough time with their next consoles which will likely cost a thousand dollars or more is my gut feeling.

↳ reply 1 — Tuna-Fish:

GPU-style platforms (lots of compute connected to a big shared pipe that connects to a large pool of fast memory) are inherently more efficient for centralized inference.

Local inference gets truly interesting when the proper next-gen, natively AI and not just a repurposed GPU, stuff starts to land. Initially things like compute-in-memory and fancy flash, and later possibly the truly exotic stuff like various RMM (read-mostly-ram, for example stacked FeFET on logic) tech.

IMO there is no chance for ubiquitous local AI to happen if that means people using GPUs. But the industry is chasing all possible solutions for more efficient inference platforms, and if something like pachinko machine architecture with FeFETs ends up winning, suddenly buying a local ai inference solution in a box is no longer as insane.

↳ reply 2 — winwang:

If consumers were willing to pay more for GPUs like datacenters do, NVIDIA would have sold plenty of consumer GPUs. Or would you press a button to halve your revenue for some reason?

(I say this as someone who would have liked a 5090...)

I don't see any difference between the conversations around self-hosting local AI and self-hosting regular software, which have been going on for decades.

Yes, there are a hundred valid reasons to self-host. But 99%+ of consumers aren't going to care.

People don't even care when the cost of hosting is ~free, like a simple home server. How many are ready to buy thousands of dollars worth of AI hardware, which could very well be obsolete a couple of years from now?
